teile.einleitung: An electrical conductor is a material that carries electric current well. This includes above all metals such as copper and aluminium. The opposite are insulators such as plastic or glass, which do not let current through.
wichtigste: Conductors are materials that carry electric current well.
The best conductors are metals such as silver, copper, gold and aluminium.
In metals there are freely moving electrons that carry the current.
Materials that do not conduct electricity are called insulators.
A cable consists of a conducting copper wire and an insulating covering.
Water with dissolved salts and the human body also conduct electricity.
Semiconductors such as silicon are the basis for computer chips.

abschnitte.text: Electric **current** is a movement of electrically charged particles. A **conductor** is a substance in which such particles can move easily. In metals these are the **electrons**, which move freely between the atoms. If you apply a voltage, they flow in one direction. This is how electricity gets from the socket to the lamp, for example.

**Silver** conducts best of all metals, but it is expensive. That is why **copper**, which conducts almost as well, is usually used for cables. For large overhead power lines, aluminium is often used because it is light. Gold does not rust and is therefore used for fine contacts in mobile phones and computers. Graphite, the material in pencils, also conducts electricity.

Substances that do not let current through are called **insulators**. These include plastic, rubber, glass, porcelain, dry wood and air. They protect us from electric current. That is why cables are covered with plastic and plugs have a plastic grip. On electricity pylons, insulators of glass or ceramic hold the lines in place.

The **human body** also conducts electricity, because it contains a lot of salty water. Current from a socket can therefore be life-threatening. Electrical devices should never be near a bath. In Switzerland the voltage at a socket is 230 volts. On the railway, the overhead line even carries electricity at 15,000 volts, which is why you must never climb on railway wagons.

Between conductors and insulators lie the **semiconductors**, for example silicon. Their conductivity can be controlled deliberately. Computer chips, light-emitting diodes and solar cells are built from them. Some substances conduct electricity at very low temperatures with no loss at all. These **superconductors** are used, for example, in the magnets at CERN near Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of electrically charged particles through a substance.
A material that does not conduct electricity, for example plastic.
A material whose conductivity can be controlled, such as silicon.
Tiny, negatively charged particles that carry the current in metals.

gewusst: Pure water hardly conducts electricity; only dissolved salts and minerals make it a conductor.
Birds can sit on a power line without danger, because the current cannot flow through their bodies into the ground.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Bernoulli was a mathematician and physicist from the famous Bernoulli family of scholars in Basel. He studied how liquids and gases flow and, in doing so, discovered the law named after him. His ideas still explain why a spray bottle works or why two sheets of paper move towards each other when you blow between them.
wichtigste: Daniel Bernoulli was born in Groningen in 1700 and died in Basel in 1782.
He came from the Bernoulli family of Basel, which produced several important mathematicians.
From 1725 he worked for a few years at the Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg.
In 1738 he published his famous book “Hydrodynamica”.
Put simply, Bernoulli's law says: the faster something flows, the lower the pressure.
He explained the pressure of a gas by the impacts of many tiny particles.
In 1760 he used statistics to calculate the benefit of vaccination against smallpox.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Bernoulli was born in **1700** in **Groningen** in the Netherlands, where his father Johann Bernoulli was a professor at the time. The family came from **Basel** and soon returned there. His uncle Jakob and his father were already famous mathematicians. Daniel studied medicine, but was mainly interested in mathematics and physics.

From **1725** Daniel Bernoulli worked at the newly founded Academy of Sciences in **St Petersburg** in Russia. There he also met the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler, who became his friend. In 1733 he returned to Basel and at first taught **anatomy and botany** at the university. Later he became professor of physiology and finally of physics.

In 1738 his book **“Hydrodynamica”** about flowing liquids appeared. It contains the basic idea of **Bernoulli's law**: the faster a liquid or gas flows, the lower the pressure. That is why, if you blow between two sheets of paper hanging close together, they move towards each other. The law also helps to understand how water flows in pipes and how air flows around aircraft wings.

Daniel Bernoulli had a bold idea: a gas consists of a huge number of tiny particles that are constantly flying around. When these particles hit a wall, **gas pressure** is created. With this he laid a foundation stone of the **kinetic theory of gases**. It was only about a hundred years later that this idea was generally accepted.

In the 18th century **smallpox** was a feared disease from which many people died. In 1760 Bernoulli used **statistics** to calculate how many years of life an early vaccination would save on average. His calculation showed that vaccination was worth it. This makes him a pioneer of the mathematical study of diseases.

Daniel Bernoulli won a prize of the Paris Academy of Sciences ten times, a great success for a researcher of his time. He also worked on probability, vibrating strings and shipbuilding. The **Bernoulli principle** is explained today in physics books all over the world. In Basel, a street and a university building still remind people of the famous Bernoulli family.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of a liquid or gas in one direction.
How strongly something pushes on a surface, for example air on a wall.
The study of how liquids move and which forces act on them.
Mathematics that collects and analyses lots of data in order to draw conclusions.

gewusst: In 1734 Daniel shared a prize of the Paris Academy with his father Johann, who was so annoyed about it that he is said to have thrown him out of the house.
As a medical student, Daniel Bernoulli wrote his doctoral thesis on breathing.

teile.einleitung: Carl Linnaeus was a Swedish naturalist who brought order to the variety of living things. He invented a system in which every plant and animal species gets a unique name made of two words. Researchers all over the world still use this system today.
wichtigste: Carl Linnaeus lived in Sweden from 1707 to 1778.
His most famous work is called Systema Naturae; the first edition appeared in 1735.
In his system a scientific species name consists of two words.
The first word names the genus, for example Canis for the wolf, Canis lupus.
Linnaeus gave humans the name Homo sapiens.
In 1758 he correctly placed whales among the mammals.
In 1732 he went on a research expedition to Lapland.

abschnitte.text: Carl Linnaeus was born in 1707 in Råshult in southern Sweden, the son of a pastor. Even as a child he loved plants; his father had a large garden. He studied medicine and later became a professor at **Uppsala University**. In 1761 he was made a nobleman and from then on called himself **Carl von Linné**.

In 1732 the young Linnaeus travelled to **Lapland** in the far north. On this journey he covered long distances, partly on foot and partly by boat. He described unknown plants and animals and observed the life of the **Sami**, the indigenous people of Lapland. His notes were later published as a book.

In 1735 the first edition of his work **Systema Naturae** appeared; at that time it was only a few pages long. In it Linnaeus divided nature into three kingdoms: animals, plants and stones. Within the kingdoms he arranged living things into levels such as class, order, genus and species. In the famous 10th edition of 1758 he placed **whales** among the mammals and not among the fish.

Before Linnaeus, plants often had long Latin descriptions as names. Linnaeus established **binomial nomenclature**: every name consists of the **genus** and a second word for the species. The wolf is called Canis lupus, and the dog belongs to the same genus Canis. Linnaeus called humans **Homo sapiens**, which means wise human.

Linnaeus had the idea of a **flower clock**, in which flowers that open and close at fixed times of day show the time. His favourite flower was the delicate **twinflower**, which bears his name: Linnaea borealis. Many of his students travelled around the world as his “apostles” and collected plants. One of them, Daniel Solander, sailed with James Cook to the South Seas.

Zoologists officially start their naming with the 10th edition of Systema Naturae from **1758**, botanists with his work Species Plantarum from 1753. Even today every newly discovered species gets a two-part name according to Linnaeus's rules. In London the **Linnean Society** bears his name and looks after his collections. Linnaeus has also appeared on Swedish banknotes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related species, for example all dog-like animals of the genus Canis.
The smallest basic unit in the system of living things, such as the wolf.
Naming every species with two Latin words.
The science of classifying living things.

gewusst: Even during his lifetime Linnaeus was called the “prince of botanists”.
The name Mammalia for the mammals comes from Linnaeus.
Linnaeus gave a scientific name to more than 10,000 plant and animal species.

teile.einleitung: The Encyclopédie was a huge French encyclopedia that began to appear in 1751. Edited by Denis Diderot and Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert, it set out to collect all the knowledge of its time and make it available to everyone. It is regarded as one of the most important works of the Enlightenment.
wichtigste: The Encyclopédie was edited by Diderot and d'Alembert.
The first volume appeared in 1751.
With its text and plate volumes it comprised 28 volumes in all.
Its aim was to make the knowledge of the time available to everyone.
It belongs to the intellectual movement of the Enlightenment.
The plate volumes showed workshops, tools and machines in especially great detail.
In 1759 the Encyclopédie was banned in France.
In Yverdon a separate, revised version in 58 volumes appeared from 1770 to 1780.

abschnitte.text: Its full title, translated, was “Encyclopedia, or a Systematic Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts, and Crafts”. The work was created in **Paris** and was originally only meant to be a translation of an English encyclopedia. Under **Denis Diderot** and **Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert** it became a completely new and much larger work. The first volume appeared in 1751 and the last in 1772. With 17 volumes of text and 11 volumes of plates, it comprised 28 volumes in all and more than 70,000 articles.

The Encyclopédie belongs to the **Enlightenment**, a movement of the 18th century. Its supporters wanted people to think for themselves and to rely on reason and observation rather than mere obedience. The encyclopedia was meant to make the **knowledge of the time** available to everyone, not just to scholars and nobles. Well-known thinkers such as Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu wrote articles. Louis de Jaucourt was especially hard-working and wrote thousands of articles.

What was new was that the Encyclopédie also took **crafts** seriously. Diderot visited workshops and had craftspeople explain to him how they worked. In the **plate volumes**, detailed copperplate engravings showed workshops, tools and machines. You can see, for example, how paper, glass or needles were made. Today these pictures are a valuable source for understanding life in the 18th century.

Many articles carefully criticised the church and the power of the king. So the Encyclopédie had powerful opponents. In 1759 it was **banned** in France, and the Pope also put it on the list of forbidden books. D'Alembert withdrew, but Diderot carried on working in secret. The remaining volumes of text appeared later as a set with a false place of printing.

The work had a great effect in Switzerland too. In **Yverdon** in the canton of Vaud, the Italian-born scholar Fortunato Bartolomeo De Felice published his own revised version from 1770 to 1780. It comprised 58 volumes and was less critical of the church than the Paris original. For that reason it was read especially in Protestant areas. Yverdon was thus an important place for books and ideas of the Enlightenment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large reference work that collects knowledge from many fields.
A movement in the 18th century that relied on reason and independent thinking.
A picture cut into a copper plate and then printed on paper.
The control or banning of books and opinions by those in power.

gewusst: Diderot worked on the Encyclopédie for more than 20 years, and in 1749, two years before the first volume, he spent several months in prison because of a critical piece of writing.
An article by d'Alembert about the city of Geneva caused a great dispute there, partly because he suggested the city should have a theatre.

teile.einleitung: In a chemical reaction, substances turn into new substances with different properties. This happens all around us all the time, for example when cooking, when things rust or when a fire burns. Even in our bodies, countless chemical reactions take place every second.
wichtigste: In a chemical reaction, substances turn into new substances.
The starting substances are called reactants, the new substances products.
The atoms are kept; they are just rearranged.
Typical signs are a change of colour, gas bubbles, heat or light.
Examples are burning, rusting, baking and digestion.
Many reactions first need a trigger, for example a spark.
Chemists describe reactions with chemical equations.

abschnitte.text: In a **chemical reaction**, substances form that did not exist before. The substances at the start are called **reactants**, the new substances **products**. Bonds between atoms are broken and new ones are formed. The atoms themselves do not disappear; they just rearrange themselves. This is different from melting ice, because water stays water.

You can often spot a reaction by a **change of colour**, for example when iron rusts brown. Sometimes gas bubbles form, for example when you mix baking powder with vinegar. Many reactions give off heat or light, like a burning match. A solid substance or a new smell can also appear. Some reactions happen so slowly that you hardly notice them.

When **burning**, wood reacts with the oxygen in the air to form carbon dioxide, water and ash. When you bake a cake, the eggs, flour and sugar change because of the heat. In our bodies, digestion breaks food down into smaller building blocks. In **photosynthesis**, plants make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. A cut apple turning brown is also a chemical reaction.

In the 18th century the French chemist **Antoine Lavoisier** showed something important by weighing very precisely. In a reaction, the mass at the end is the same as at the start. This is called the **law of conservation of mass**. When wood burns it seems to disappear, but the substances escape into the air as gases. In a closed container the weight would stay the same.

Chemists write reactions down using formulas. One example is the reaction of hydrogen with oxygen to form water. It is written as 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. The reactants are on the left, the products on the right, and the arrow shows the direction. There must be the same number of atoms of each kind on both sides.

Many reactions do not start by themselves; they need **activation energy**. A match only lights when you strike it on the rough strip. Heat speeds up most reactions and cold slows them down, which is why food keeps longer in the fridge. A **catalyst** is a substance that makes a reaction faster without being used up itself. In the body, enzymes do this job.

begriffe.erklaerung: A starting substance that is used up in a reaction.
A new substance that is formed in a reaction.
The energy needed for a reaction to start.
A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up in it.

gewusst: The fireworks on Swiss National Day on 1 August glow in many colours because different metal salts give off coloured light in the reactions.
In every cell of your body, thousands of chemical reactions take place at the same time every second.

teile.einleitung: CERN is the largest research centre for particle physics in the world. It lies near Geneva, right on the border between Switzerland and France. There, thousands of researchers study what the world is made of at the very smallest scale.
wichtigste: CERN is a European organisation for nuclear research based in Geneva.
It was founded in 1954, and Switzerland was part of it from the start.
The largest particle accelerator, the LHC, is a ring 27 kilometres long.
The LHC lies about 100 metres underground and reaches into France.
In 2012 the Higgs particle was detected at CERN.
The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in 1989.
Researchers from more than 100 countries work together at CERN.

abschnitte.text: The name **CERN** comes from the French “Conseil européen pour la recherche nucléaire”. The organisation was founded in 1954 by twelve European countries, including Switzerland. It was meant to bring researchers from Europe back together after the Second World War. Today more than 20 countries are members. The site lies in **Meyrin** near Geneva and stretches across the border into France.

The most important machine is the **Large Hadron Collider**, or LHC for short. It is a ring-shaped tunnel 27 kilometres round and lies about 100 metres below the ground. Inside it, tiny particles called **protons** are accelerated to almost the speed of light. Powerful magnets keep them on their circular path, and for this the magnets are cooled to almost minus 271 degrees Celsius. The LHC started operating in 2008.

In the LHC, particles coming from opposite directions are made to crash into each other. These **collisions** create new particles for tiny moments. Huge measuring devices, the **detectors**, record everything. The ATLAS detector is about as tall as a seven-storey building. Computers all over the world analyse the enormous amounts of data.

On 4 July 2012, CERN announced the detection of the **Higgs particle**. This particle explains why other particles have mass. The physicists Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize for it in 2013. **Antimatter** is also produced and studied at CERN. As early as the 1980s, important particles such as the W and Z bosons were discovered here.

In 1989 the British computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** proposed a system for sharing documents at CERN. This became the **World Wide Web** with web pages and links. The world's first website went online at CERN in 1991. CERN made the technology freely available in 1993 so that everyone could use it at no cost. Without this invention, the internet as we know it would not exist.

CERN is one of the most important research sites in Switzerland. Visitors can see an exhibition in the new Science Gateway visitor centre. The wooden building called the **Globe** is a well-known landmark in front of the site. Many school classes from Switzerland visit CERN every year. CERN is also a big employer for Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the very smallest building blocks of matter.
A machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus of an atom.
A particle detected in 2012 that explains why things have mass.
A measuring device that records particles and their tracks.

gewusst: The protons in the LHC whizz around the 27 kilometre ring more than 11,000 times in one second.
The computer that ran the first website had a note on it asking people not to switch it off.

teile.einleitung: First aid is the first set of measures with which you help an injured or suddenly ill person until experts arrive. It includes calling for help, calming the person down and knowing some simple techniques. Anyone can give first aid, including children.
wichtigste: At an accident you first pay attention to your own safety.
The ambulance emergency number in Switzerland is 144.
The air rescue service Rega can be reached on 1414.
The number 112 works throughout Europe and also in Switzerland.
In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on the number 145.
An unconscious person who is breathing normally is placed in the recovery position.
Small burns are cooled at once with cool water.

abschnitte.text: Before you help, you look around carefully and pay attention to your **own safety**. On a road, for example, you put up a warning triangle or stay at the edge. Then you think about what has happened and who needs help. Only after that do you act, call for help and look after the injured person.

For an ambulance you dial **144**, for the police 117 and for the fire brigade 118. Rega with its rescue helicopters can be reached on 1414. The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland. In cases of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** gives advice on 145 around the clock.

On the phone you say calmly **where** something has happened, what has happened and how many people are injured. You only hang up when the person taking the emergency call says so. After that you stay with the injured person, talk to them and comfort them. Just listening and staying there helps many people a great deal.

If a person does not react, you check whether they are breathing normally. If they are breathing, you place them in the **recovery position** so that the airways stay clear. You cover them up and watch their breathing until help arrives. If they are not breathing, you start **chest compressions** and, if possible, have someone fetch a defibrillator.

A small **burn** is cooled for about ten to twenty minutes with cool, but not ice-cold, water. With a nosebleed you bend the head slightly forward and press the nostrils together. Tipping the head back is wrong, because the blood then runs into the throat. Small grazes are rinsed clean and covered with a plaster.

In Switzerland everyone has to attend a **first aid course** to get a learner driving licence. Courses are offered, for example, by Samaritan associations and the Swiss Red Cross. There are also special courses for children in which you practise in a playful way. If you practise regularly, you stay calmer in an emergency.

begriffe.erklaerung: A telephone number on which you get help straight away.
A position in which an unconscious person lies safely on their side and can breathe freely.
A device that can use an electric shock to bring a fluttering heart back into the right rhythm.
Rhythmic pressing on the chest so that the blood keeps flowing.

gewusst: Modern defibrillators speak and explain step by step what you should do.
The emergency numbers 144, 117, 118 and 112 can be called on a mobile phone even without credit.
In Switzerland you can even be committing an offence if you do nothing although you could help.

teile.einleitung: The endosymbiotic theory explains where important parts of our cells come from. It says that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria that were taken in by a larger cell and went on living inside it. Out of this cooperation came the complex cells of plants, animals and fungi.
wichtigste: The biologist Lynn Margulis made the theory well known from 1967.
As early as 1905 the Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski suggested that chloroplasts descend from symbionts.
Chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria.
According to current knowledge, mitochondria descend from alphaproteobacteria.
Mitochondria have their own ring-shaped DNA, like bacteria.
New chloroplasts only form by the division of existing plastids.
When a cell takes in an alga that already has chloroplasts, this is called secondary endosymbiosis.

abschnitte.text: The cells of animals, plants and fungi contain small components called **organelles**. Two of them are special: the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell, and the **chloroplasts**, in which plants carry out photosynthesis. According to the endosymbiotic theory, these organelles used to be independent bacteria. A larger cell took them in but did not digest them. Instead the two lived together and both gained from it.

Living together for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**. If one partner lives inside the other, it is called **endosymbiosis**. The bacterium that was taken in got protection and nutrients. In return the host cell got plenty of energy, or, with chloroplasts, sugar from sunlight. Over time the bacteria handed many of their genes over to the cell nucleus and could no longer live on their own.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own **ring-shaped DNA**, just like bacteria. They have their own **70S ribosomes**, which resemble the ribosomes of bacteria and are smaller than the cell's other ribosomes. They are surrounded by two envelopes, which fits with having been taken in. New chloroplasts and mitochondria only form by the division of existing ones; the cell cannot build them from scratch. Comparisons of genes show that chloroplasts descend from **cyanobacteria** and mitochondria from alphaproteobacteria.

As early as 1905 the Russian botanist **Konstantin Mereschkowski** suggested that chloroplasts descend from symbionts. For a long time this idea was hardly noticed or even laughed at. In 1967 the US biologist **Lynn Margulis** published an article that put the theory on a new footing. Her work was at first rejected by many scientific journals. Only when the DNA of the organelles could be studied did the theory become accepted, and today it is regarded as well supported.

The taking in of cyanobacteria by a cell is called **primary endosymbiosis**. From it came green algae, red algae and later land plants. Some cells later took in a whole alga that already had chloroplasts of its own; this is **secondary endosymbiosis**. Diatoms and the eyespot flagellate came about in this way, for example. These events were a very long time ago, with the taking in of mitochondria probably well over a billion years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small component in a cell with a particular job.
The power station of the cell, which gets energy from food.
A green organelle in which plants make sugar from sunlight.
Two living things living together in a way that benefits both.

gewusst: In each of your cells, often hundreds to thousands of mitochondria are at work, which were once bacteria.
There is a sea slug that takes chloroplasts from the algae it eats into its body and lets them carry on photosynthesis for a while.

teile.einleitung: The candela is the unit of measurement for luminous intensity, in other words how strongly a light source shines in a particular direction. It is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units. Its name comes from the Latin word for candle.
wichtigste: Luminous intensity is measured in candelas.
The Latin word “candela” means candle.
A candle flame has a luminous intensity of roughly 1 candela.
The unit symbol of the candela is cd.
The candela is the SI base unit that takes into account how sensitive the human eye is.
Its definition uses green light.
Related units are the lumen for the amount of light and the lux for how brightly a surface is lit.

abschnitte.text: The **candela** measures **luminous intensity**, that is, how brightly a light source shines in a particular direction. Its symbol is **cd**. The name comes from the Latin word for candle. An ordinary candle flame really does shine with about one candela.

The candela is one of the seven **SI base units**, together with the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole. All other units can be derived from these base units. The candela is the only one that has to do with the human eye. It takes into account how sensitive our eyes are to different colours.

Our eyes are most sensitive to **green light**. That is why the definition of the candela uses green light with a precisely fixed frequency. Red or blue light with the same energy looks less bright to us. So the candela does not simply measure energy, but brightness as we perceive it.

Besides the candela there are two related units. The **lumen** tells you how much light a lamp gives off in total; you can find it on the packaging of LED bulbs, for example. The **lux** measures how brightly a surface is lit, such as a school desk. For comfortable reading, a desk needs a lot more lux than a corridor.

In the past, light was compared with real candles, but candles never burn exactly the same. So different countries had different candle units, for example the Hefner candle in Germany. Around the middle of the 20th century, countries agreed internationally on the candela. Since then its definition has been made more precise several times.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a light source shines in a particular direction.
Unit for the total amount of light a lamp gives off.
Unit for how brightly a surface is lit.
Internationally agreed units of measurement that are used almost everywhere in the world.

gewusst: A powerful lighthouse can reach a luminous intensity of many hundreds of thousands of candelas.
The brightness of mobile phone and computer screens is often given in candelas per square metre.
The candela is the only SI base unit that is based on human perception.

teile.einleitung: Epidemiology is the science that studies how often diseases occur, who they affect and why. It counts the sick, compares groups and looks for causes. In this way it helps to prevent diseases and to keep whole populations healthy.
wichtigste: Epidemiology studies the spread and the causes of diseases in the population.
John Snow, who traced a source of cholera in London in 1854, is regarded as its founder.
Incidence measures the new cases in a particular period.
Prevalence says how many people are ill at a particular time.
Case fatality says what share of those who fall ill die of a disease.
Cohort studies follow groups of people over many years.
In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health monitors the spread of infectious diseases.

abschnitte.text: The word **epidemiology** comes from Greek and means roughly “the study of what comes upon the people”. While a doctor treats an individual person, epidemiologists look at whole groups. They ask, for example: how many people have flu, at what age, in what place? They study not only infectious diseases but also heart disease, allergies or accidents. Their most important tool is numbers and **statistics**.

In 1854 hundreds of people in the London district of Soho died of **cholera** within a few days. At the time many people believed that bad air caused the disease. The doctor **John Snow** marked the deaths on a street map and saw that they clustered around a water pump in Broad Street. He had the pump handle removed, and the number of new cases fell. For this, Snow is regarded as the founder of modern epidemiology.

**Incidence** counts the new cases in a period. If 30 out of 10,000 people in a town fall ill in one year, that is 300 cases per 100,000 people. **Prevalence** says what share of the population is ill at a particular time. **Case fatality** says how many of those who fall ill die of the disease. A disease that occurs with a steady, similar frequency in a region is called endemic; if it suddenly spreads strongly, it is called an epidemic, or, worldwide, a pandemic.

In a **cohort study**, a group of people is followed over years and it is recorded who newly falls ill. If, for example, 1,000 smokers are compared with 1,000 non-smokers and 40 fall ill against 10, the **relative risk** is 4. In this way the Britons Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill showed around 1950 that smoking causes lung cancer. Researchers have to watch out for **confounders**, that is, hidden factors that create an apparent link. Someone who buys lighters more often, for example, does not have a higher cancer risk because of the lighters but because they smoke.

In Switzerland, doctors and laboratories must report certain infectious diseases to the **Federal Office of Public Health**. In this way it is noticed early when, for example, measles or flu are spreading. During the Covid-19 pandemic from 2020, epidemiological figures were in the news every day. Well-known research centres are the universities of Bern, Zurich, Basel, Geneva and Lausanne. The Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Allschwil near Basel studies diseases such as malaria worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of new cases of a disease in a particular period.
The share of people who are ill at a particular time.
When a disease suddenly occurs much more often in a region than usual.
A hidden disturbing factor that can create a false link.
A group of people that a study follows over a longer time.

gewusst: John Snow's map with the cholera deaths is regarded as one of the most famous maps in the history of science.
In London today there is a replica of the old pump without a handle at the spot.
The Framingham study in the USA has been following the residents of a small town and their descendants since 1948.

teile.einleitung: The kingfisher is a small bird with a brilliant blue back and an orange belly that lives by streams, rivers and lakes. It dives into the water at lightning speed to catch small fish. Its beak is so well shaped that it inspired engineers in Japan to build a better high-speed train.
wichtigste: The kingfisher has a brilliant blue back.
It eats mainly small fish.
It dives into the water almost without a splash.
In Switzerland you can watch it by streams, rivers and lakes.
It makes its nest in a tunnel in an earth bank.
A Japanese high-speed train was given a nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak.
The train with the new nose no longer made a loud tunnel boom and used less electricity.

abschnitte.text: The **kingfisher** is about as big as a sparrow, but looks stocky because of its large head and short tail. Its back shines **blue** to turquoise, and its belly is orange-red. The blue does not come from pigment but from tiny structures in the feathers that bend the light. Its long, pointed beak looks like a dagger. Because of its colours it is also called a “flying jewel”.

The kingfisher lives by slow-flowing, clear **streams, rivers and lakes**. In Switzerland you see it mainly on the Swiss Plateau, for example on the Aare, the Reuss or the Rhine. It needs clear water so that it can see the fish. It also needs branches above the water from which it can hunt. In very cold winters, when the waters freeze over, it can hardly find food, and many kingfishers die.

The kingfisher eats mainly **small fish**, and also water insects and tadpoles. It sits still on a branch and watches the water. When it sees a fish, it plunges in head first and enters the water **almost without a splash**. With the fish in its beak it flies back to the branch and knocks it against the wood. Then it swallows it head first.

The kingfisher does not build its nest in trees but in a **tunnel in a steep earth bank**, usually right by the water. With their beaks the parents dig a tunnel that is often half a metre long or more. At the end there is a small chamber in which the female lays several white eggs. The young are fed with fish until they can fly. Because many rivers have been straightened, such natural steep banks are often missing today.

In Japan the **Shinkansen** high-speed train used to enter tunnels at high speed. In doing so it pushed the air ahead of it, and on leaving the tunnel there was a loud **boom**. The engineer Eiji Nakatsu, a birdwatcher, thought of the kingfisher, which moves from water to air without a splash. The train was given a long nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak. The new train was quieter and faster and used less electricity, an example of **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology that copies solutions from nature.
A colour created by tiny structures instead of by pigment.
A steep bank of earth or sand by a river or lake.
Hunting in which an animal waits quietly and then strikes at lightning speed.

gewusst: The kingfisher can hover on the spot in flight above the water, rather like a helicopter.
The German name Eisvogel probably does not come from the word for ice but from an old word for shining or shimmering.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Kahneman was an Israeli-American psychologist who studied how people make decisions and why they often make thinking errors in the process. Although he was a psychologist, he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. His book about fast and slow thinking became a bestseller around the world.
wichtigste: Daniel Kahneman lived from 1934 to 2024.
He received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002.
With Amos Tversky he developed prospect theory in 1979.
Loss aversion means that losses hurt more than gains of the same size give pleasure.
In his 2011 book “Thinking, Fast and Slow” he describes two systems of thinking.
System 1 works quickly, automatically and intuitively; System 2 works slowly and deliberately.
With Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein he wrote the book “Noise”.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Kahneman was born in **Tel Aviv** in 1934 and grew up in Paris. As a Jewish child he survived the German occupation there during the Second World War. Later he studied psychology in Jerusalem and in the USA. Among other places he taught at **Princeton University**, and he died in March 2024.

From the late 1960s Kahneman worked closely with the psychologist **Amos Tversky**. Together they showed that people often do not decide as sensibly as economists assumed. They described many **judgement heuristics**, that is, rules of thumb we use to decide quickly but which can lead to mistakes. Tversky died in 1996 and so could no longer receive the Nobel Prize.

In 1979 the two published **prospect theory**. A key idea is **loss aversion**: if you lose 100 francs, you are more upset than you would be pleased about winning 100 francs. That is why people sometimes take unusual risks just to avoid a loss. For this work Kahneman received the **Nobel Prize in Economics** in 2002.

In his 2011 book “Thinking, Fast and Slow”, Kahneman describes two ways of thinking. **System 1** works quickly, automatically and intuitively, for example when you instantly recognise an angry face. **System 2** works slowly and with effort, for example when you work out 17 times 24. Many thinking errors happen when System 1 answers, although System 2 would really be needed.

In the **Linda problem**, many people think “bank clerk and feminist” is more likely than just “bank clerk”. That is impossible and is called the **conjunction fallacy**. The **peak-end rule** says that we judge experiences mainly by their high point and their end. In the book “Noise”, Kahneman and colleagues studied how much the judgements of experts vary by chance.

Kahneman is regarded as one of the founders of **behavioural economics**, which combines psychology and economics. His findings are used in medicine, politics, finance and advertising. If you know about these thinking errors, you can make some decisions more consciously. His book has been translated into many languages and has sold millions of copies.

begriffe.erklaerung: Losses feel worse than gains of the same size feel good.
A simple rule of thumb for deciding quickly.
A gut feeling that arises without long thought.
Research into how people really make economic decisions.

gewusst: Kahneman never attended a course in economics and still received the Nobel Prize in Economics.
According to the peak-end rule, a long visit to the doctor can be remembered as better if it ends gently.
Kahneman stressed that even experts like himself are not protected against these thinking errors.

teile.einleitung: Decomposers are living things that break down dead plants, animals and waste. They turn these remains back into minerals that plants need to grow. Without them the world would be buried under leaves and dead animals.
wichtigste: Decomposers break down dead living things and waste in an ecosystem.
The most important decomposers are bacteria and fungi.
The breakdown of organic substances into minerals is called mineralisation.
Without decomposers, dead plants and animals would pile up.
Soil animals such as the earthworm shred leaves and mix up the soil.
In a compost heap, decomposers produce nutrient-rich compost.
In the cold, decomposers work more slowly, which is why leaves break down more slowly in mountain forests.

abschnitte.text: The German word for decomposer, **Destruent**, comes from the Latin word for “to destroy”. In an **ecosystem** there are three big groups: **producers** such as plants make food, consumers such as animals eat it, and decomposers break down the remains. In this way the cycle of substances is closed. What was once a leaf later becomes food for a new plant again.

The most important decomposers are **bacteria** and **fungi**, which can often only be seen under a microscope. Fungi run through the forest floor with fine threads and dissolve wood and leaves. Then there are soil animals such as earthworms, woodlice, millipedes and springtails. They shred the remains so that bacteria and fungi can work better.

The **earthworm** pulls leaves into its burrows and eats them together with soil. In doing so it shreds the leaves and mixes the soil thoroughly. Its burrows loosen the earth and let air and water in. Charles Darwin even wrote a whole book about the work of earthworms.

Decomposers break down **organic substances** such as sugars and proteins step by step. In the end, water, carbon dioxide and **minerals** such as nitrogen and phosphorus compounds are left. This process is called **mineralisation**. Plants take up the minerals with their roots and use them to grow.

A **compost heap** is a small decomposer factory. Vegetable scraps, grass cuttings and leaves are broken down there by microorganisms and soil animals. The microorganisms release **heat** as they work, which is why it gets warm inside a fresh heap. After a few months, dark, nutrient-rich compost forms, a natural fertiliser.

How fast decomposers work depends on warmth and moisture. In the warm Swiss Plateau, leaves break down much faster than in cold **mountain forests**. At high altitudes, needles and branches therefore lie around for a long time and form thick layers. Many municipalities collect green waste, which is processed further in large composting plants or biogas plants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A habitat with all the living things that live in it and depend on one another.
The breakdown of dead material into simple minerals that plants can take up.
A living thing such as a plant that makes its own food using sunlight.
A tiny living thing such as a bacterium that can only be seen with a microscope.

gewusst: A handful of soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
Inside a large compost heap it can get so hot that you would not want to keep your hand in it for long.

teile.einleitung: Carl Gustav Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist and one of the best-known researchers of the human mind in the 20th century. He founded analytical psychology and coined terms such as introversion, extraversion and archetypes. Many of his ideas are still alive today in psychology, art and everyday life.
wichtigste: Carl Gustav Jung was born in 1875 in Kesswil in the canton of Thurgau.
As a young doctor he worked at the Burghölzli clinic in Zurich under Eugen Bleuler.
At first he was close friends with Sigmund Freud, but they broke off around 1913.
He called his own school analytical psychology.
He described a collective unconscious with primal images shared by all people, the archetypes.
He made the terms introversion and extraversion well known.
Jung died in 1961 in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.

abschnitte.text: Carl Gustav Jung was born in 1875 in **Kesswil** on Lake Constance in the canton of **Thurgau**. His father was a pastor. He grew up near Schaffhausen and Basel and studied medicine in Basel. Even as a child he was interested in dreams and the mysteries of the mind.

From 1900, Jung worked at the **Burghölzli** psychiatric clinic in Zurich under the famous psychiatrist **Eugen Bleuler**. There he studied how people react to words and developed tests for this. Later he opened his own practice in **Küsnacht** on Lake Zurich. He lived there until his death in 1961.

In 1907 Jung met the Viennese doctor **Sigmund Freud**, the founder of psychoanalysis. The two became close friends, and at first Freud saw Jung as his successor. But Jung soon had his own ideas about the unconscious. Around 1913 they broke off their friendship, and Jung went his own way.

Jung called his school **analytical psychology**. He believed that besides the personal unconscious there is also a **collective unconscious** that all people share. It contains primal images, which he called **archetypes**, such as the “shadow” or the “wise old man”. Such figures appear in myths, fairy tales and dreams from all over the world.

Jung made the terms **introversion** and **extraversion** well known. Introverted people tend to draw strength from quiet and from their inner world. Extraverted people tend to recharge their energy by being with others. Today these terms are used quite naturally in everyday life.

Jung also coined the term **synchronicity** for meaningful coincidences that happen at the same time without one causing the other. His ideas influenced psychology, literature, art and the study of religion. In Küsnacht there is the C. G. Jung Institute, where specialists are trained. However, many of his theories are disputed in science because they are hard to test.

begriffe.erklaerung: A doctor who treats people with mental illnesses.
Part of the mind whose contents we are not directly aware of.
A primal image that appears in stories and dreams of all cultures.
Turning towards one's own inner world.
A meaningful coincidence in time of events without a direct connection.

gewusst: Jung built himself a stone tower in Bollingen on the Upper Lake of Zurich, where he withdrew to think.
His personal “Red Book” with his own pictures and texts was only published in 2009, almost 50 years after his death.
Well-known personality tests are partly based on Jung's division of people into different types.

teile.einleitung: Conrad Gessner was a doctor and naturalist from Zurich who lived in the 16th century and wanted to know almost everything. He wrote an enormous book of animals, collected knowledge about plants, stones, languages and books, and climbed mountains when hardly anyone did. He is regarded as one of the most important scholars in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Conrad Gessner lived in Zurich from 1516 to 1565.
He worked as the town doctor in his home city.
His great book of animals is called Historia animalium.
He is regarded as the father of bibliography because he listed thousands of books and authors.
In 1555 he climbed and described Mount Pilatus near Lucerne.
He was one of the first to describe the pencil and the tulip.
In 1565 he died of the plague.
He appeared on the 50 franc note of the sixth series of banknotes.

abschnitte.text: Conrad Gessner was born in **Zurich** in 1516; his family was poor. Thanks to grants he was able to study in France and in Basel and became a doctor. Back in Zurich he taught natural history at the Hohe Schule, the forerunner of the university. From 1554 he worked as the **town doctor** of Zurich.

Gessner's most famous work is the **Historia animalium**, which appeared from 1551 in several thick volumes. In it he collected everything that was known at the time about mammals, birds, fish and amphibians. The book contained hundreds of **woodcuts**, that is, printed pictures, including Albrecht Dürer's famous rhinoceros. Besides real animals, it also includes fabulous creatures such as the unicorn, because at that time people could not yet tell everything apart for certain.

In 1545 Gessner published the **Bibliotheca universalis**. In it he listed thousands of books and authors who had written in Latin, Greek and Hebrew. Because it was the first large book catalogue of this kind, Gessner is regarded as the **father of bibliography**. In another work he compared more than a hundred languages of the world.

In the 16th century people rarely climbed mountains for pleasure, and many were afraid of them. Gessner, on the other hand, raved about the beauty of the Alps. In 1555 he climbed **Mount Pilatus** near Lucerne and described the trip in a report. He is therefore seen as an early **lover of mountains** and a pioneer of mountaineering.

Gessner collected and drew many plants and created his own garden. In 1559 he was one of the first in Europe to describe and draw a **tulip**, which he had seen in a garden in Augsburg. In his book on stones and fossils from 1565, he was one of the first to describe a **pencil**, a graphite stick in a wooden case. In the same year he died in Zurich of the **plague**, which he had been treating as a doctor.

The Swiss National Bank honoured Gessner on the **50 franc note** of the sixth series, which was in circulation from 1978. It also showed animals and plants from his works. In Zurich, the Gessnerallee is named after him. Many plants and animals carry his name in their scientific names.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who studies and describes animals, plants and stones.
A list of books and writings on a subject.
A picture carved into wood and then printed on paper.
A dangerous infectious disease that killed many people in the past.

gewusst: Gessner resolved to climb at least one mountain every year.
Gessner's book of animals was reprinted and translated into other languages long after his death.
The plant genus Gesneria, after which the gesneriad family is named, is a reminder of him.

teile.einleitung: The ETH Domain is a group of six universities and research institutes that belong to the federal government. They include ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne as well as four well-known research institutes. Together they are among the most important places of science in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The ETH Domain consists of six universities and research institutes.
The two universities are ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne.
In addition there are PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag.
They belong to the federal government, and the legal basis is the ETH Act.
The Federal Council sets strategic goals for four years at a time.
CERN in Geneva is not part of the ETH Domain.
The Paul Scherrer Institute runs large research facilities such as the SLS and SINQ.

abschnitte.text: The ETH Domain is a group of six institutions that belong to the **federal government**. Its legal basis is the **ETH Act** of 1991. The Federal Council sets strategic goals for four years at a time. The group is run and supervised by the ETH Board.

**ETH Zurich** was founded in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic. Albert Einstein studied here and later taught here too. **EPFL** in Lausanne has been a federal university since 1969. Both are among the best technical universities in the world.

The **Paul Scherrer Institute** (PSI) lies in Villigen in the canton of Aargau. It is the largest research institute for the natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. In the **Swiss Light Source** (SLS), electrons circle in a storage ring and produce very intense X-ray light. With the neutron source SINQ, researchers can look inside materials.

**WSL** in Birmensdorf studies forests, snow and landscape, and the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos is part of it. **Empa** does research on new materials and technologies, for example in Dübendorf and St Gallen. **Eawag** studies lakes, rivers and drinking water. In this way the institutes cover many important topics for Switzerland.

**CERN** near Geneva is also a famous research centre. However, it is not part of the ETH Domain but an international organisation of many states. The cantonal universities such as Bern, Basel or Geneva do not belong to it either. These universities are supported mainly by the cantons.

Tens of thousands of people study, teach and do research in the ETH Domain. Many new companies, known as **spin-offs**, come out of this research. The institutes work on questions such as climate change, energy, health and natural hazards. In this way the ETH Domain contributes a great deal to Switzerland's prosperity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A federal institute of technology, a university belonging to the federal government.
An institute where research is the main activity and there is less teaching.
The body that runs and supervises the whole ETH Domain.
A new company that comes out of a university or a research institute.

gewusst: The abbreviation EPFL stands for “École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne”.
The Paul Scherrer Institute is named after the Swiss physicist Paul Scherrer.
The avalanche bulletin for the Swiss Alps comes from the SLF in Davos, which is part of the ETH Domain.

teile.einleitung: El Niño is a climate phenomenon in the tropical Pacific in which the sea off South America becomes much warmer. It occurs every few years and changes the weather across half the world. Droughts, floods and forest fires can be the result.
wichtigste: El Niño is Spanish and means “the Christ child”.
The cool opposite phase, with especially cold water in the eastern Pacific, is called La Niña.
During an El Niño the trade winds weaken or partly reverse.
Off Peru the fishing industry suffers, because cold, nutrient-rich deep water no longer rises.
In Indonesia and Australia a strong El Niño often brings dry weather and forest fires.
El Niño occurs roughly every 2 to 7 years.
A strong El Niño temporarily raises the global average temperature.

abschnitte.text: Fishermen on the coast of **Peru** noticed long ago that the sea sometimes becomes warmer around Christmas time. They called this current **El Niño**, Spanish for “the Christ child”. Later researchers realised that behind it lies a great interplay between sea and air. The opposite phase with especially cold water is called **La Niña**, “the girl”. Together with the changes in air pressure, the whole phenomenon is called ENSO.

Normally the **trade winds** blow from east to west over the tropical Pacific. They push warm surface water towards Indonesia and Australia. Off South America, cold deep water rises in its place. During an El Niño the trade winds weaken or partly reverse. Then the warm water sloshes back to the east, and the Pacific off South America becomes unusually warm.

Researchers measure the water temperature with buoys, ships and satellites. An area of sea in the middle of the Pacific, the **Niño 3.4** region, is especially important. If the temperature there is at least 0.5 degrees above the long-term average, the US weather service NOAA speaks of El Niño conditions. El Niño occurs roughly every **2 to 7 years** and usually lasts about a year. Because it builds up slowly, it can often be forecast months in advance.

Off Peru the cold, **nutrient-rich** deep water is missing during an El Niño, so there is less plankton and fewer fish. At the same time, heavy rain with flooding often falls on the coast of Peru and Ecuador. In **Indonesia** and **Australia**, on the other hand, it becomes dry and the danger of forest fires rises. In Africa, India and South America too, rainy and dry seasons change. In Europe and Switzerland, by contrast, the effects are small and hard to prove.

During a strong El Niño the Pacific gives off a lot of heat to the air. This temporarily raises the **global average temperature**. There were especially strong events in 1997/98 and 2015/16, for example. The El Niño of 2023/24 also contributed to 2024 being a record year worldwide for temperature. Researchers are studying whether El Niño is changing because of global warming.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wind in the tropics that almost always blows from the same direction.
The cool opposite phase to El Niño, with cold water in the eastern Pacific.
Cold water from the depths of the sea, often rich in nutrients.
Short for El Niño and the Southern Oscillation, the whole interplay of sea and air.

gewusst: El Niño can affect the price of cocoa, coffee and rice all over the world, because harvests fail.
During an El Niño some deserts in Peru and Chile turn green, because it suddenly rains there.

teile.einleitung: A chatbot is a computer program you can have a conversation with by text or voice, almost as if it were a person. Modern chatbots like ChatGPT are based on large language models that have learned from huge amounts of text. They can do an astonishing amount, but they also make mistakes.
wichtigste: A chatbot is a program that talks with people in natural language.
One of the first chatbots was ELIZA, which Joseph Weizenbaum developed in the 1960s.
ChatGPT became available to the public at the end of 2022.
GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.
At its core, a large language model predicts the most likely next piece of a word.
The input or instruction you give a chatbot is called a prompt.
Made-up information that sounds convincing is called a hallucination.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the English “chat” and **“bot”**, short for robot. So a chatbot is a computer program that talks with people. You type in a question or say it aloud, and the program answers. Chatbots can be found on company websites, in apps, in voice assistants and in learning programs.

In the 1960s the computer scientist **Joseph Weizenbaum** developed the program **ELIZA** at MIT in the USA. In its best-known version, ELIZA played a psychotherapist and asked questions back, such as “Tell me more about your family”. The program did not really understand anything; it just looked for key words. Even so, some people believed they were talking to an understanding partner, which worried Weizenbaum a great deal.

Today's chatbots are based on **large language models**. These are trained with huge amounts of text from books and the internet. At its core, such a model always predicts the **most likely next piece of a word** and so builds up an answer sentence by sentence. The abbreviation GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer, that is, a pre-trained model that produces texts.

The American company OpenAI made **ChatGPT** available to the public at the end of 2022, and within a few months millions of people around the world were using it. Other companies' chatbots soon followed, for example Claude, Gemini and Copilot. They can write texts, translate, create programs and explain questions. Swiss schools and universities are also discussing how such tools can be used sensibly.

The input or instruction you give a chatbot is called a **prompt**. The more precise the prompt, the better the answer usually fits. But chatbots can invent information that sounds convincing; this is called a **hallucination**. That is why you should always check important information in reliable sources.

A chatbot is not a person, even if it sounds friendly and personal. You should not trust it with private data such as your address, passwords or photos of yourself. For homework, a chatbot can help by explaining things, but thinking for yourself is still important. According to their rules, many services may only be used from a certain age or with your parents' permission.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer program you can talk with by text or voice.
A computer program that has learned from many texts how to produce language.
The input or instruction you give a chatbot.
When a chatbot invents false information that sounds real.
Computer programs that solve tasks which would otherwise need human thinking.

gewusst: ELIZA was named after Eliza Doolittle, a character in the play “Pygmalion” who learns to speak in a posh way.
As early as 1950 the mathematician Alan Turing proposed a test in which you have to find out whether you are writing to a person or a machine.
Language models do not read texts in whole words but in small pieces of words called tokens.

teile.einleitung: The Coriolis force is a fictitious force that seems to push movements on the rotating Earth off to the side. It makes sure that winds do not blow in straight lines and that tropical storms spin. It is named after the French scientist Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis.
wichtigste: The Coriolis force arises because the Earth rotates and we move with it.
It is a fictitious force that only appears in a rotating frame of reference.
In the northern hemisphere it deflects movements to the right, in the southern hemisphere to the left.
At the equator the horizontal Coriolis force is zero; at the poles it is greatest.
The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ω sin φ, where φ is the latitude.
If the speed of a parcel of air doubles, the Coriolis force doubles too.
It is far too weak to affect water draining out of a bath.

abschnitte.text: The Earth spins once a day on its own axis. If you are standing on the Earth you notice nothing, because you turn with it. But if something moves over long distances, such as air or sea water, it seems to be **deflected** from its path. This apparent force is called the **Coriolis force**, after Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis, who described it in 1835.

Imagine you throw a ball to a friend on a spinning roundabout. Seen from above, the ball flies straight, but your friend turns away, and to you on the roundabout its path looks curved. This is exactly how the Coriolis force works; it only appears in a **rotating frame of reference**. That is why it is called a **fictitious force**.

Its strength depends on the speed and on the place on Earth. What matters is the **Coriolis parameter** f = 2Ω sin φ, where Ω is the rotation speed of the Earth and φ is the latitude. At the **equator**, sin φ is zero, so there is no horizontal deflection there. It is greatest at the poles, and at 30 degrees latitude it is exactly half as strong as there.

In the northern hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects air to the right. That is why air does not flow straight into an area of low pressure but circles around it anticlockwise. In the southern hemisphere it is the other way round. In the free atmosphere the **geostrophic wind** even blows parallel to the **isobars**, the lines of equal air pressure on the weather map.

You often hear that water in a bath in the northern hemisphere always drains in a particular direction. That is not true, because for such small amounts and short distances the Coriolis force is far too weak. The shape of the bath and the tiniest movements in the water are much more important. It only plays a decisive role in large systems such as **ocean currents** and weather systems.

In 1851 Léon Foucault used a long pendulum in Paris to show that the Earth rotates. The plane in which a **Foucault pendulum** swings slowly turns during the day, because the Earth turns beneath it. You can see such pendulums in many museums and universities. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss also have to take the Coriolis force into account in their weather models.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that only an observer who is moving along notices, because their own viewpoint is moving.
The viewpoint from which you describe a movement.
Lines on a weather map that join places with the same air pressure.
A measure of how far north or south of the equator a place is.

gewusst: No tropical storms form right at the equator, because the Coriolis force that sets them spinning is missing there.
Switzerland lies at about 47 degrees north; there the Coriolis force is already almost three quarters as strong as at the North Pole.

teile.einleitung: Deep Blue was a chess computer made by the company IBM. In 1997 it defeated the reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match of six games. This victory is regarded as a milestone in the history of artificial intelligence.
wichtigste: Deep Blue was developed by the company IBM.
In the first match in 1996, world champion Garry Kasparov won.
In the rematch in New York in 1997, Deep Blue won by 3.5 to 2.5.
For the first time a reigning world champion lost a match against a computer.
Deep Blue found its moves mainly by calculating many positions ahead at lightning speed.
The computer could check about 200 million positions per second.
After the victory, Deep Blue was not developed any further.

abschnitte.text: **Deep Blue** was a huge special computer built only for chess. It consisted of cabinets full of computers with specially developed **chess chips**. The idea came from students at Carnegie Mellon University who later continued their work at **IBM**. One of the most important developers was Feng-hsiung Hsu.

Deep Blue did not understand chess like a human. It calculated at lightning speed what would happen on the board after many possible moves, up to about **200 million positions** per second. It judged each position with a formula, for example by material and the safety of the king. On top of that came stored **openings** and advice from chess grandmasters who helped the team.

In February **1996** Deep Blue played world champion **Garry Kasparov** in Philadelphia. The computer won the very first game, which caused a great stir. In the end, however, Kasparov won clearly by 4 to 2. Afterwards the IBM team improved the computer considerably.

In May **1997** there was a rematch over six games in **New York**. Deep Blue won by **3.5 to 2.5**, with two wins, three draws and one defeat. Kasparov was very disappointed and demanded another rematch. IBM refused and ended the project.

For the first time a reigning **world champion** lost a whole match against a computer under tournament conditions. The victory showed how powerful computing power can be, even though Deep Blue did not learn by itself. Today even chess programs on a mobile phone play better than any human. Modern programs such as AlphaZero even taught themselves to play chess by playing against themselves.

After the match, Deep Blue was no longer needed. Parts of the computer are now on display in **museums** in the USA. The match has been retold in books and films. Kasparov himself later wrote a book about artificial intelligence and now sees computers as helpers for people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer or program that can play chess.
A tie in chess; each side gets half a point.
How many calculation steps a computer can manage in a certain time.
The first moves of a chess game, for which there are well-known patterns.

gewusst: At the time, Kasparov suspected that people had secretly helped the computer, but there was never any proof of this.
The name Deep Blue refers to its predecessor “Deep Thought” and to IBM, which is nicknamed “Big Blue”.

teile.einleitung: Citizen science means that lay people, in other words people who are not professional researchers, help with real science. They count birds, sort galaxies in photos or solve puzzles in online games. Anyone can take part, including children and teenagers.
wichtigste: Citizen science means lay people taking part in research.
In the Galaxy Zoo project, volunteers classify galaxies by their shape.
Foldit is an online game in which you fold proteins.
The Zooniverse platform brings together many such projects.
BirdLife Switzerland runs the hands-on campaign “Hour of Garden Birds”.
The University of Zurich and ETH Zurich jointly run a Citizen Science Center.
With citizen science data, you have to watch out for varying data quality.

abschnitte.text: In citizen science, **volunteers** work together with researchers. They collect observations, analyse photos or provide computing power. In this way, amounts of data come together that experts alone could never manage. The idea is actually old: centuries ago, **lay people** were already recording the weather or collecting plants and beetles.

In 2007 the **Galaxy Zoo** project started, in which volunteers classified galaxies in telescope pictures by their shape. This led to the **Zooniverse** platform, which now has many projects, from counting penguins to old handwritten documents. In **SETI@home**, millions of participants made the computing power of their computers available to search radio signals from space. The project ran from 1999 to 2020.

**Foldit** is an online game in which you fold **proteins** into the right shape like a puzzle. In 2011 players worked out the structure of a protein in just a few weeks, a problem experts had puzzled over for a long time. The result helped with research into viruses. The players were even named as co-authors of a scientific publication.

In BirdLife Switzerland's **Hour of Garden Birds**, people count the birds in their garden or park for one hour. The **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** relies heavily on observations by volunteers for its breeding bird atlases. The **Citizen Science Center Zurich**, run by the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich, helps to set up new projects that people can join. You can also take part in projects on wild bees, hedgehogs or air quality.

Citizen science produces a lot of data and connects science with the public. Participants learn a great deal about nature and research. One risk is varying **data quality**, because not everyone observes or identifies things equally well. That is why reports are checked, and photos or apps help to avoid mistakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who has not learned something as their profession.
Collected information such as numbers, observations or photos.
An important building block of living things.
A huge collection of billions of stars, like our Milky Way.

gewusst: The Christmas Bird Count in North America has been running since 1900 and is one of the oldest citizen science projects.
A Dutch teacher discovered a mysterious green gas cloud in Galaxy Zoo, which was named Hanny's Voorwerp after her.
Many plant and bird apps on mobile phones also pass their observations on to researchers.

teile.einleitung: Christiaan Huygens was a scientist from the Netherlands who lived in the 17th century. He invented the accurate pendulum clock, discovered Saturn's moon Titan and explained light as a wave. This makes him one of the most important scientists of his time.
wichtigste: Christiaan Huygens lived from 1629 to 1695 and came from The Hague in the Netherlands.
In 1655 he discovered Saturn's largest moon, Titan, with a telescope he had built himself.
He was the first to realise that Saturn's “handles” are a thin, flat ring.
In 1656 he invented the pendulum clock, which kept time much more accurately than all earlier clocks.
In 1675 he presented the balance spring, which is found in almost every mechanical wristwatch today.
Huygens held the idea that light travels as a wave.
In 1657 he wrote one of the first textbooks on probability.

abschnitte.text: Christiaan Huygens was born in The Hague in **1629** and died there in **1695**. His father, Constantijn Huygens, was a well-known poet and diplomat who gave his children an excellent education. Christiaan studied law and mathematics in Leiden and Breda. Even as a young man he was interested in mathematics, optics, astronomy and mechanics.

Together with his brother, Huygens ground his own lenses and used them to build better **telescopes**. In this way, in 1655, he discovered Saturn's moon **Titan**, the largest moon of Saturn. Other astronomers had seen strange “handles” on Saturn and could not explain them. Huygens realised that they were a thin, flat **ring** that surrounds the planet without touching it.

Before Huygens, clocks were often wrong by many minutes a day. In 1656 he invented the **pendulum clock**, in which a swinging pendulum sets the beat. Because a pendulum always takes the same time for one swing, clocks suddenly became very accurate. In 1675 he also presented the **balance spring**, which made small portable watches more accurate. The Swiss watch industry still benefits from this today.

Huygens imagined that **light** spreads out in a similar way to waves on a pond. Every point of a wave is itself the starting point of new small waves; this is called **Huygens' principle**. With it he could explain how light is refracted and reflected. His book about light appeared in 1690; at the same time Isaac Newton held the idea that light is made of particles.

In 1657 Huygens wrote one of the first textbooks on **probability**, the mathematics of chance, for example when rolling dice. From 1666 he lived in **Paris** and was a leading member of the newly founded Academy of Sciences. He worked there for many years and exchanged ideas with the best scientists in Europe. Later he returned to the Netherlands.

Huygens combined careful observation with mathematics and is therefore seen as a pioneer of modern **physics**. His inventions in timekeeping were essential for centuries. A space probe was named “Huygens” in his honour. In 2005 it landed on Saturn's moon **Titan**, which he had discovered about 350 years earlier.

begriffe.erklaerung: A weight on a string or rod that swings evenly back and forth.
A small wheel in mechanical watches that swings back and forth with a spiral spring and sets the beat.
A vibration that spreads out, like circles on the surface of water.
The part of mathematics that works out how likely a chance event is.

gewusst: The Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005; it was the first landing on a moon in the outer solar system.
Huygens even wrote a book in which he wondered whether there could be life on other planets.

teile.einleitung: Chromosomes are tiny structures in the cell nucleus in which the genetic information of a living thing is packed. You can imagine them like volumes in a library that contain the building plans for the whole body. Each species has a typical number of chromosomes.
wichtigste: Chromosomes consist of DNA wound around proteins.
Humans have 46 chromosomes, that is 23 pairs, in almost every body cell.
A chimpanzee has 48 chromosomes, a dog 78.
Chromosomes are easiest to see during cell division.
A doubled chromosome consists of two chromatids joined at the centromere.
The protective caps at the ends are called telomeres.
In Down syndrome, chromosome 21 is present three times.

abschnitte.text: In every **cell nucleus** there is a long thread of genetic material, the **DNA**. So that this thread fits, it is wound around tiny protein balls and tightly coiled. These packages are the chromosomes. They carry thousands of **genes**, which help to decide things like eye colour or the shape of the nose.

Humans normally have **46 chromosomes**, arranged in 23 pairs. The two chromosomes of a pair match in shape and genes and are called **homologous chromosomes**. A chimpanzee has 48 chromosomes, a dog 78 and a potato 48. But the number says nothing about how complex a living thing is.

Before a cell divides, the chromosomes are doubled. Such a chromosome then looks like an X and consists of two identical halves, the **chromatids**. They are joined at a narrow point, the **centromere**. At the ends are the **telomeres**, which protect against damage like the plastic tips on shoelaces.

If you arrange a photo of all the chromosomes of a cell by size, you get a **karyogram**. Doctors can see from it whether a chromosome is missing or there is one too many. In **Down syndrome**, chromosome 21 is present three times instead of twice; this is called trisomy 21. People with Down syndrome often learn a little more slowly, but many lead active and independent lives.

In the 19th century, researchers stained cells and saw thread-like structures in the nucleus. Around 1880 the German doctor Walther Flemming observed closely how they behave during cell division. In 1888 the anatomist Wilhelm Waldeyer gave them the name **chromosome**, which means coloured body. It was only in 1956 that it was firmly established that humans have 46 chromosomes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule in which genetic information is stored.
A section of DNA with the building plan for a particular feature.
The control centre of a cell, where the chromosomes are found.
An ordered picture of all the chromosomes of a cell.
A protective cap at the end of a chromosome.

gewusst: If you unrolled the DNA from a single human cell, the thread would be about two metres long.
For a long time researchers believed humans had 48 chromosomes, until they counted more carefully in 1956.
Some ferns have more than 1,000 chromosomes in one cell.

teile.einleitung: Deep learning is a method of artificial intelligence in which computers learn from many examples using artificial neural networks. It is behind face recognition on mobile phones, voice assistants, translation programs and chatbots. The word deep refers to the many layers of these networks.
wichtigste: “Deep” refers to the many layers of a neural network, one behind the other.
For image recognition, convolutional neural networks, or CNNs, are especially common.
In 2012 the network AlexNet clearly won the ImageNet competition and triggered a breakthrough.
Deep networks are usually trained on graphics processors, because they carry out many calculations in parallel.
Hinton, LeCun and Bengio received the 2018 Turing Award for their work.
Residual networks use shortcut connections that skip layers.
In transfer learning, a pre-trained model is adapted to a new task.

abschnitte.text: Deep learning is part of **machine learning**. Instead of programming exact rules into a computer, you show it a huge number of examples, such as millions of photos of cats and dogs. An **artificial neural network** made of many computing nodes, the neurons, learns from them by itself what a cat looks like. The model is roughly the brain, in which nerve cells are connected to one another.

A deep network consists of many **layers** one after another. The first layers recognise simple things such as edges and colours; later layers recognise eyes, ears and finally whole faces. During training, the connections are improved step by step using a method called **backpropagation**. A problem can occur here: with the **vanishing gradient**, the corrections in early layers become so small that these layers hardly learn any more.

**Convolutional networks** are especially suitable for images, because they use small filters to recognise local patterns. In 2012 the convolutional network **AlexNet** won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin; in this competition, programs had to sort images into a thousand categories. This is regarded as the breakthrough of deep learning. In 2015 **residual networks** with shortcut connections made much deeper networks possible, with more than a hundred layers.

Deep networks are usually trained on **graphics processors**, or GPUs, which were actually built for video games. They calculate many matrix operations at the same time. **Batch normalisation** standardises the intermediate values of a layer and makes training more stable. In transfer learning, you take a model that has already been trained and adapt it to a new task with just a few examples.
