The ideas behind neural networks are decades old, but for a long time there was not enough data and computing power. **Geoffrey Hinton**, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio received the 2018 Turing Award, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science, for their pioneering work. In 2024 Hinton, together with John Hopfield, even received the Nobel Prize in Physics. Important contributions came from Switzerland: Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber of the **IDSIA** research institute in Lugano developed the LSTM network for language and time series in 1997.

Deep learning is found in translation programs, speech recognition, photo filters and self-driving cars. In 2016 the program **AlphaGo** beat one of the best players of the board game Go. Large **language models** such as chatbots are also based on deep networks. Because such systems make mistakes and use a lot of electricity, people are also discussing risks and rules.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer program made of many connected computing nodes that learns from examples.
The learning phase in which a network is improved with many examples.
Graphics processing unit, a chip that carries out many calculations at the same time.
A model that has already been trained learns a new, similar task.

gewusst: The ImageNet image database contains more than 14 million photos labelled by people.
Graphics processors for video games became the most important tool of artificial intelligence.
A large language model has many billions of adjustable numbers, known as parameters.

teile.einleitung: Dian Fossey was an American researcher who devoted her life to the mountain gorillas of Africa. She observed these shy great apes for almost twenty years in the mountain forests of Rwanda. Through her fight against poachers she did a great deal to protect the gorillas.
wichtigste: Dian Fossey lived from 1932 to 1985 and came from San Francisco in the USA.
Before her research she worked as an occupational therapist.
In 1967 she founded the Karisoke research station in Rwanda.
She studied mountain gorillas and won their trust with great patience.
She fought determinedly against poachers.
In 1977 her favourite gorilla, Digit, was killed by poachers.
Her book “Gorillas in the Mist” was made into a film in 1988.
With Jane Goodall and Biruté Galdikas she formed a famous trio of women researchers.

abschnitte.text: Dian Fossey was born in **San Francisco** in **1932**. At first she worked as an **occupational therapist** with children. On a trip to Africa in 1963 she saw mountain gorillas for the first time and was fascinated. Later the famous researcher Louis Leakey encouraged her to study the animals over a long period.

In **1967** Fossey founded the **Karisoke** research station in **Rwanda**. It lies in the Virunga volcanoes between the mountains Karisimbi and Visoke, hence the name. The area is cool and damp and often wrapped in mist. She lived there for many years in simple huts in the middle of the mountain forest.

**Mountain gorillas** are very shy and live in family groups with one large male, the silverback. Fossey copied their sounds and behaviour, such as chewing plants. In this way the animals got used to her and let her come close. She showed that gorillas are peaceful, social animals and not wild monsters, as many people believed at the time.

The gorillas were threatened by **poachers**, who set traps or killed animals. Fossey destroyed traps and took very determined action against poaching. In 1977 her favourite gorilla, **Digit**, was killed by poachers. After that she set up a fund to protect the gorillas better.

In 1983 her book **“Gorillas in the Mist”** was published, and in 1988 it was made into a film with Sigourney Weaver. At the end of 1985 Dian Fossey was killed in her hut at Karisoke; the crime was never fully solved. She was buried in the graveyard near the station, next to her gorillas. Her gravestone says that no one loved gorillas more than she did.

Thanks to protection measures and research, the number of mountain gorillas has risen again, to more than 1,000 animals (as of about 2018). But they are still considered **endangered**. Gorilla tourism now brings Rwanda money and helps to preserve the forests. The foundation that grew out of Fossey's fund still does research in Rwanda.

begriffe.erklaerung: A subspecies of gorilla that lives only in mountain forests in eastern Africa.
Someone who illegally hunts or traps animals.
An adult male gorilla with silvery grey fur on his back, who leads the group.
Treatment that helps people to relearn or improve everyday skills.

gewusst: Dian Fossey, Jane Goodall and Biruté Galdikas were supported by Louis Leakey and are sometimes called “Leakey's Angels”.
Fossey gave her gorillas names such as Digit, Uncle Bert or Peanuts and knew each animal by its face.

teile.einleitung: Emotions are feelings such as joy, fear, anger or sadness that are with us all the time in everyday life. They arise in the brain, show in the face and also change the body, for example the heartbeat. Emotions help us to react quickly to dangers and opportunities and to connect with other people.
wichtigste: Paul Ekman originally named six basic emotions, including disgust.
The amygdala in the brain is especially important for recognising threats and feeling fear.
In 1872 Charles Darwin wrote a book about the expression of the emotions in man and animals.
Ekman's research in Papua New Guinea showed that basic feelings are shown in similar ways in the face all over the world.
Many brain areas involved in feelings are counted as part of the limbic system.
The psychologist Robert Plutchik designed the “wheel of emotions”.
Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognise your own and other people's feelings and to deal with them well.

abschnitte.text: An **emotion** is a short, strong reaction to something that matters to us. It has several parts: a feeling, a reaction in the body, a facial expression and often the urge to do something. With fear, the heart beats faster, the muscles tense and you want to run away. Emotions usually last only seconds to minutes. Longer-lasting states of feeling are called **moods**.

The US psychologist **Paul Ekman** originally named six **basic emotions**: joy, sadness, anger, fear, disgust and surprise. Later he added contempt. In the 1960s he visited people in Papua New Guinea who had hardly any contact with the rest of the world. They recognised the facial expressions in photos just as people in the USA did. This showed that basic feelings are shown in similar ways in the face all over the world.

Many areas of the brain are involved in feelings, and they are often counted as part of the **limbic system**. The **amygdala**, an almond-shaped nucleus deep in the brain, is especially important. It recognises threats at lightning speed and triggers fear, sometimes before we consciously think. The front part of the cerebral cortex then helps to control and judge feelings. Messenger substances such as dopamine and stress hormones such as adrenaline also play a part.

In 1872 the naturalist **Charles Darwin** wrote a book about the expression of the emotions in man and animals. He found that dogs, cats and monkeys also show their feelings with their bodies. The psychologist **Robert Plutchik** arranged eight basic feelings in a colourful “wheel of emotions”. In it, opposite feelings such as joy and sadness face each other. In Switzerland, the University of Geneva is an important centre of emotion research.

All feelings are normal and have a purpose, including unpleasant ones such as anger or fear. Anger shows, for example, that something feels unfair, and fear protects against danger. The ability to recognise your own and other people's feelings and to deal with them well is called **emotional intelligence**. It helps to put feelings into words, to breathe deeply or to talk to someone you trust. If you understand other people's feelings, you can put yourself in their place better; this is called **empathy**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic feeling that all people in the world know and show in similar ways.
A small, almond-shaped area in the brain that is important in fear.
A group of brain areas that are strongly involved in feelings and memories.
The ability to share in the feelings of other people.

gewusst: People born blind also smile when they are happy, even though they have never seen a smile.
The word emotion comes from the Latin “emovere”, which means “to move out”.

teile.einleitung: Epigenetics studies how outside influences control the activity of genes without changing the DNA sequence itself. You can picture it like switches or bookmarks on the DNA. It explains, for example, why completely different cells arise from the same genetic information.
wichtigste: Epigenetics studies how genes are switched on and off.
The order of the DNA building blocks stays unchanged.
Small chemical markings on the DNA act like switches.
Diet, stress, exercise and the environment can influence these markings.
Thanks to epigenetics, the same DNA produces skin cells, nerve cells or muscle cells.
Identical twins become more and more different epigenetically over the course of their lives.
The prefix “epi” comes from Greek and means “on top of” or “above”.

abschnitte.text: Almost every cell in your body contains the same **DNA** with all the genes. All the same, a skin cell is completely different from a nerve cell. This is because only certain genes are active in each cell. **Epigenetics** studies how this selection is controlled. The DNA sequence, that is, the actual text of the genetic information, stays the same.

You can picture DNA as a gigantic cookery book. Epigenetic markings are like paper clips or sticky notes that decide which recipes are read. One important marking is **DNA methylation**, in which small methyl groups are attached to the DNA. Usually they switch a gene off. The proteins around which the DNA is wound, the **histones**, can also be changed and make the genes easier or harder to read.

Epigenetic markings can change over the course of a life. Researchers are studying how **diet**, exercise, stress, smoking or sleep affect them. Identical twins have the same DNA but become more and more different epigenetically as they get older. This may explain why one of them gets an illness and the other does not. However, many of these connections are not yet fully understood.

A well-known example is **honeybees**. A queen and a worker can hatch from exactly the same kind of egg. The larva that becomes the queen gets plenty of **royal jelly**, a special food. This changes which genes are active, and she becomes bigger and can lay eggs. The fur colour of tortoiseshell cats is also connected with the switching off of genes.

The term epigenetics was coined by the British biologist **Conrad Hal Waddington** in 1942. Since about 2000, epigenetics has been a fast-growing field of research. It is important for cancer research, because in cancer cells genes are often wrongly switched on or off. Some medicines already act on epigenetic markings. Whether and how strongly such markings are passed on to children is still being studied.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA with the building instructions for a particular feature.
Whether a gene is currently being read and used or is switched off.
The attaching of small chemical groups to the DNA, which usually switches genes off.
Proteins around which the DNA is wound like a thread around a spool.

gewusst: Almost all the cells in your body have the same DNA, and yet there are more than 200 different types of cell.
Whether a bee larva becomes a queen or a worker is decided above all by its food.

teile.einleitung: An ice age is a long period in which the Earth was much colder than today and huge glaciers covered large parts of the land. During the last ice age almost all of Switzerland lay under ice. Mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses and cave bears lived here at that time.
wichtigste: In the last ice age, glaciers covered almost all of Switzerland.
In Valais the ice was more than 1,000 metres thick.
The last ice age came to an end about 12,000 years ago.
Glaciers carved out many Swiss lakes, for example Lake Zurich.
Valleys shaped by a glacier have a U-shape.
The mammoth, the woolly rhinoceros and the cave bear lived in the ice age.
The people of the ice age often hunted reindeer.

abschnitte.text: An **ice age** is a phase of Earth's history in which there are large masses of ice on the continents. In the current ice age, **cold periods** and **warm periods** have been alternating for about 2.6 million years. In the cold periods the glaciers grew far out into the lowlands, and in the warm periods they melted back. We live today in a warm period that began about 12,000 years ago. Because there are still huge ice sheets in Greenland and the Antarctic, strictly speaking our time also counts as part of an ice age.

At the peak of the last cold period, about 20,000 years ago, enormous glaciers flowed from the Alps into the Swiss Plateau. In Valais the ice was more than 1,000 metres thick, and only the highest peaks stuck out. The Rhone Glacier reached beyond Geneva and Solothurn, and the Rhine Glacier far beyond Lake Constance. On average it was probably about 10 degrees colder than today. Because so much water was locked up in ice, the sea level worldwide was about **120 metres** lower.

The glaciers shaped the Swiss landscape strongly. They carved out **U-shaped valleys**, such as the Lauterbrunnen valley, and dug hollows in which lakes such as Lake Zurich, Lake Geneva or Lake Lucerne now lie. At the edges of the glaciers, hills of rubble were left behind, the **moraines**. Huge boulders that the ice carried far away are called **erratic boulders**. Many erratic boulders now lie in the middle of the Swiss Plateau, even though their rock comes from the Alps.

In the cold steppe in front of the glaciers lived **mammoths** with long, dense fur and curved tusks. The **woolly rhinoceros**, reindeer, wild horses, musk oxen and cave lions were also about. The **cave bear** was bigger than a brown bear and hibernated in caves, for example in the Wildkirchli in the Alpstein. In Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich, many mammoth bones were found that can now be seen in a small museum. Many of these animals died out at the end of the ice age.

The people of the ice age lived as **hunters and gatherers** and followed the herds of animals. The reindeer was especially important, providing meat, hides, bones and antlers for tools. In the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen, tools and a famous engraved drawing of a reindeer were found. People lived in caves, under rock overhangs or in tents made of hides. They went hunting with spear throwers and later with bows and arrows.

For a long time nobody could explain how the erratic boulders got into the lowlands. In the 19th century Ignaz Venetz from Valais and Jean de Charpentier suspected that huge glaciers had carried them there in the past. The Swiss-born researcher **Louis Agassiz** made the idea of an ice age known worldwide from 1837. Today we know that small changes in the Earth's orbit around the sun set off the cold and warm periods. This explanation goes back to the Serbian researcher Milutin Milanković.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large mass of ice that slowly moves down the valley.
A ridge of stones and rubble left behind by a glacier.
A large boulder that a glacier has carried far from where it came from.
A warmer period between two cold periods, like today.

gewusst: During the ice age you could walk from France to England, because the sea level was so low.
The German name for an erratic boulder, Findling, comes from the idea that these stones lie in the landscape like foundlings.
In Siberia, mammoths have been found that were preserved in the frozen ground with their fur and skin.

teile.einleitung: An ice core is a long column of ice that researchers drill out of a glacier or an ice sheet. The ice is like an archive: layer by layer it stores information about the climate and the air of times gone by. Some ice cores tell of times hundreds of thousands of years ago.
wichtigste: An ice core is a long column of ice from a glacier or ice sheet.
Tiny air bubbles in the ice show what the air was made up of in the past.
From different oxygen atoms in the ice, the temperature of that time can be estimated.
Dark layers can show ash from volcanic eruptions.
In the Alps, researchers take ice cores at Colle Gnifetti in the Monte Rosa massif.
Ice cores are stored in very cold rooms so that they do not melt.
The “Ice Memory” project preserves ice from melting glaciers for the future.

abschnitte.text: When snow stays on a glacier, it is covered year after year by new snow and pressed into ice. This creates many layers one on top of the other, and the deepest are the oldest. With a hollow **drill**, researchers pull out long cylinders of ice, usually about as thick as an arm. These pieces are labelled and kept in order. Together they make up an **ice core**, which is sometimes several kilometres long.

Tiny **air bubbles** are trapped in the ice. They contain air from the time when the ice formed. Researchers can measure in them how much carbon dioxide and methane there used to be in the air. In this way we know that before industrialisation the air contained about 280 ppm of carbon dioxide. Today it is more than 420 ppm (as of 2024), more than at any time in the last 800,000 years.

Water contains different kinds of oxygen atoms, which are called **isotopes**. Their ratio in the ice depends on how cold it was when the snow fell. In this way researchers can estimate the temperature of past times. Thin dark layers can be **ash** from volcanic eruptions, which can often be matched to a particular eruption. In some cores you can even make out individual years from light and dark annual layers.

The University of Bern is known worldwide for ice core research. The Bern physicist **Hans Oeschger** developed methods for studying the air from the ice. Researchers from Bern took part in major drilling projects in Greenland and the Antarctic, such as the EPICA project, whose ice reaches back about 800,000 years. The Paul Scherrer Institute also drills in the Alps, for example at **Colle Gnifetti** in the Monte Rosa massif at more than 4,000 metres. There the ice shows, for example, how air pollution in Europe has changed.

Ice cores are stored in cold rooms at very low temperatures so that they do not melt and their information is preserved. However, many glaciers in the Alps and other mountains are melting so fast that their archive will soon be lost. The **Ice Memory** project is therefore drilling ice cores from threatened glaciers. These are to be kept in a snow cave near the Concordia research station in the Antarctic, where it is naturally very cold. In this way future researchers will still be able to study the ice with better methods.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge cover of ice that covers a whole country, as in Greenland and the Antarctic.
A version of an atom that is slightly heavier or lighter.
Parts per million: it says how many out of a million particles of air are a particular substance.
A natural store from which the climate of earlier times can be read.

gewusst: In ice cores from Greenland, traces of lead from Roman times are found, when a lot of metal was smelted in Europe.
Some ice cores from the Antarctic are more than three kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Vinegar is a sour liquid used for seasoning, preserving and cleaning. It owes its sour taste to acetic acid, which tiny bacteria make from alcohol. Vinegar is one of the oldest seasonings used by people.
wichtigste: Vinegar contains acetic acid, which gives it its sour taste.
Acetic acid bacteria turn alcohol, for example in wine, into vinegar.
Table vinegar usually contains about five to six per cent acetic acid.
Mixed with oil, vinegar makes a simple salad dressing.
In the home, vinegar helps against limescale.
The shell of a raw egg dissolves in vinegar after about two days.
There are many kinds, such as wine vinegar, cider vinegar or balsamic vinegar.

abschnitte.text: Vinegar is mainly water with a little **acetic acid** in it. The acid gives it its typical sour taste and sharp smell. Table vinegar usually contains only about five to six per cent acid. There is also **vinegar essence**, which is much stronger and may only be used diluted.

Vinegar is made when **acetic acid bacteria** use oxygen from the air to turn alcohol into acetic acid. This process is called **fermentation**. That is why wine left standing open turns sour over time and finally into vinegar. On fermenting vinegar a slimy skin of bacteria sometimes forms, which is called the mother of vinegar. Today vinegar is made in large tanks into which air is blown.

Depending on the starting material there is **wine vinegar**, cider vinegar, rice vinegar or herb vinegar. Especially famous is the dark **balsamic vinegar** from the area around Modena in Italy, some of which matures in wooden barrels for years. In cooking, vinegar gives salads, sauces and soups a fresh note. For a simple salad dressing you mix vinegar with oil, salt and a little mustard.

Acid stops many bacteria and fungi from growing. That is why vegetables such as cucumbers, onions or beetroot are put into vinegar, which is called **pickling**. In this way food keeps for a long time. People in ancient times already knew this method, long before there were fridges.

abschnitte.titel: Vinegar in the home and in an experiment
abschnitte.text: Vinegar dissolves **limescale**, which is why it is used to clean taps or descale a kettle. You can show this with an experiment: if you put a raw egg in vinegar, small bubbles rise. The eggshell is made of lime and dissolves after about two days. What is left is a rubbery egg held together only by a thin membrane.

begriffe.erklaerung: The acid that makes vinegar sour.
The transformation of substances by bacteria or yeasts.
A slimy layer of acetic acid bacteria that can form on vinegar.
A white mineral that builds up in kettles, for example.

gewusst: The English word vinegar comes from French words meaning “sour wine”.
The bubbles in the egg experiment are carbon dioxide, which forms when the acid attacks the lime.
If you mix vinegar with baking powder it foams up strongly, a trick often used for volcano experiments.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. To find their way through this huge span of time, experts divide the history of the Earth into eras and periods. Each section has its own rocks, plants and animals.
wichtigste: The history of the Earth is divided into large sections of time.
The Precambrian covers about 88 per cent of the whole history of the Earth.
After it come the Palaeozoic, the Mesozoic and the Cenozoic.
The Mesozoic consists of the Triassic, the Jurassic and the Cretaceous.
We live today in the Cenozoic era.
The Quaternary, with its ice ages, continues to this day.
Many periods are named after rocks or mountain ranges.

abschnitte.text: Geologists read the history of the Earth from **layers of rock** and fossils. Lower layers are usually older than upper ones. Where the animal and plant world changes strongly, experts draw a boundary. This is how the geological **eras** came about, and also the smaller sections, the periods.

The **Precambrian** reaches from the formation of the Earth about 4.6 billion years ago to about 540 million years ago. It covers about 88 per cent of the whole history of the Earth. In this time the first living things arose, tiny single-celled organisms in the sea. Only towards the end were there larger, soft animals without bones or shells.

The **Palaeozoic** consists of the Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous and Permian. In the Cambrian, many animal groups with hard shells suddenly appeared. Later, plants and animals conquered the land. In the **Carboniferous**, huge swamp forests grew, from which large deposits of coal formed.

The **Mesozoic** lasted from about 252 to about 66 million years ago. It is divided into the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous and was the time of the dinosaurs. The name Triassic refers to three typical layers of rock, and the Jurassic is named after the Jura mountains. The Cretaceous takes its name from the white limestone rock chalk.

66 million years ago a large asteroid struck the Earth, and the large dinosaurs died out. With that the **Cenozoic** began, the era in which we live today. Mammals and birds now spread widely. For about 2.6 million years the **Quaternary** has lasted, with several ice ages in which glaciers also covered the Swiss Plateau.

At **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino you find famous fossils of marine reptiles and fish from the Triassic. The mountain is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the Jura there are limestone layers full of ammonites and even footprints of dinosaurs. The Alps themselves were only folded up into a high mountain range in the Cenozoic.

begriffe.erklaerung: Remains or traces of living things from earlier times that have turned to stone.
A section within a geological era, for example the Jurassic.
An expert who studies rocks and the history of the Earth.
A time in which very many animal and plant species disappear in a short period.

gewusst: If the whole history of the Earth were a single day, humans would only have existed for a few seconds before midnight.
The biggest mass extinction did not happen with the dinosaurs but about 252 million years ago at the end of the Permian.
An international body decides which boundaries and names are official in the geological time scale.

teile.einleitung: CRISPR/Cas9 is a method of genetic engineering that lets you change sections of DNA in a targeted way. It is often called “gene scissors”, because it cuts the genetic material at a precisely chosen place. Two researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for discovering it.
wichtigste: CRISPR/Cas9 makes it possible to change sections of DNA in a targeted way.
The method is often called gene scissors.
Originally, CRISPR is a defence system that bacteria use against viruses.
Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna presented the method in 2012.
The two received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 2020.
The gene scissors are used in research, medicine and plant breeding.
Changing the genetic material of humans raises difficult ethical questions.

abschnitte.text: **CRISPR/Cas9** is a tool researchers can use to change the **DNA** of living things. DNA contains the building instructions of a living thing, rather like a very long text. With CRISPR/Cas9 you can find a particular word in this text and cut it out. Then the cell can repair the spot, or a new piece can be inserted. That is why people speak of **gene scissors** or genome editing.

The system originally comes from **bacteria**. When a virus attacks a bacterium, the bacterium stores a small piece of the virus DNA in its own genetic material. If the same virus attacks again, the bacterium recognises it by this piece. The protein **Cas9** then cuts up the virus DNA. The word CRISPR is an English abbreviation for these repeating sections in the genetic material of bacteria.

The gene scissors consist of two parts. A short piece of **RNA** acts as a search template and guides the scissors to the right place in the DNA. The protein Cas9 cuts through both strands of the DNA there. The cell tries to mend the cut, which switches off or changes a gene. The method is much simpler, faster and cheaper than earlier techniques.

The Frenchwoman **Emmanuelle Charpentier** and the American **Jennifer Doudna** published their groundbreaking work in 2012. They showed that the bacterial scissors can be programmed to cut any desired place in DNA. In 2020 they jointly received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. It was the first time that two women alone shared a Nobel Prize in science. Other researchers also contributed important findings.

In research, the gene scissors help to understand what job a gene has. In **medicine**, a first therapy for the inherited blood disease sickle cell anaemia was approved in 2023. In farming, plants could be bred that are better able to resist diseases or drought. In Switzerland there has been a moratorium, that is, a temporary ban, on growing genetically modified plants since 2005. How the new breeding methods should be handled is being debated in politics.

With CRISPR you could also change the genetic material of embryos, and the changes would be inherited. In 2018 a researcher in China announced that he had changed the genetic material of babies. This was sharply condemned around the world, and he had to go to prison. Many countries, including Switzerland, ban such changes to the **germline**. Experts are discussing where the limits of this powerful technology should lie.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule that carries the genetic information of a living thing.
A section of DNA with the building instructions for a particular feature.
Methods used to change the genetic material of living things in a targeted way.
The cells whose genetic material is passed on to offspring.

gewusst: The gene scissors are so precise that they can find exactly the right spot among billions of DNA building blocks.
Yoghurt bacteria were important for research into CRISPR, because food scientists wanted to protect them from viruses.

teile.einleitung: The gut flora is the huge community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that lives in our gut. Trillions of these tiny lodgers help us to digest food, make vitamins and protect us from germs. Today experts usually speak of the gut microbiome.
wichtigste: The gut flora consists of the microorganisms in the gut.
Most gut bacteria live in the large intestine.
Roughly trillions of microorganisms live in a person's gut.
Gut bacteria help to break down dietary fibre.
Among other things, they can make vitamin K.
Useful bacteria take up space and nutrients and so keep germs away.
Antibiotics can disturb the gut flora and kill many bacteria.

abschnitte.text: In the past, bacteria were counted as plants, which is why people speak of **flora**. Today the whole community of gut inhabitants is usually called the **microbiome**. It includes bacteria, but also fungi and other tiny living things. About as many bacteria live in a person's gut as the body has cells, that is, many **trillions**.

In the stomach it is very acidic because of stomach acid, and only a few bacteria survive there. Further along in the small intestine there are more. By far the most gut bacteria live in the **large intestine**, where the mushy food moves along slowly. Every person has their own mixture of several hundred kinds of bacteria.

Gut bacteria break down **dietary fibre** from vegetables, fruit and wholegrain foods, which our body cannot digest on its own. This produces substances that nourish the gut wall. Some bacteria make **vitamin K**, which is important for blood clotting. The gut flora also trains the **immune system**.

Useful bacteria take up the space and nutrients in the gut. So germs hardly have a chance to settle there. However, a course of **antibiotics** kills not only harmful bacteria but also useful ones. Afterwards you may get diarrhoea until the gut flora has recovered.

The bacterium **Escherichia coli** normally lives harmlessly in the gut and is one of the most important research subjects in biology. It is named after the children's doctor Theodor Escherich, who described it in 1885. **Bifidobacteria** are also part of the natural gut flora and are often added to yoghurts. Such living bacteria in food are called probiotics.

A varied diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit, pulses and wholegrain foods is good for the gut flora. Fermented foods such as yoghurt or sauerkraut also contain useful bacteria. Researchers are currently studying how the gut flora is linked to being overweight, allergies and even mood. But much of this is not yet properly understood.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the microorganisms that live together in one place in the body.
The last big section of the gut, where especially many bacteria live.
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing.
A food with living, useful bacteria.

gewusst: All the bacteria in the gut together weigh about as much as a bar of chocolate up to a pack of butter.
A large part of the mass of faeces consists of bacteria.
Escherichia coli is one of the best-studied living things in the world.

teile.einleitung: The polar bear is the king of the Arctic and one of the largest predators living on land. It is perfectly adapted to ice, snow and icy sea water. But because the sea ice is melting, it is now in danger.
wichtigste: Polar bears live around the North Pole in the Arctic.
Under its white fur, the polar bear has black skin.
A thick layer of fat and its dense fur protect it from the cold.
It likes best to hunt seals, which it catches from the sea ice.
Polar bears are excellent swimmers and can swim very long distances.
The cubs are born in winter in a snow den.
Polar bears and penguins never meet in nature, because penguins live in the southern hemisphere.

abschnitte.text: A fully grown male usually weighs 350 to 600 kilograms, and some even more. Standing upright it can be almost three metres tall, while females are considerably smaller. The hairs of its fur are actually transparent and hollow; they only look white because of the light. Underneath there is **black skin**, which absorbs the sun's warmth well, and a layer of **fat** up to ten centimetres thick. The big paws have fur and small **bumps** on the soles, so the polar bear hardly ever slips on the ice.

Polar bears live in the **Arctic**, that is, around the North Pole. They are found in Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Russia and on the Norwegian islands of Svalbard. They spend a lot of time on the **sea ice** that covers the Arctic Ocean in winter. Their scientific name Ursus maritimus means “sea bear”. Penguins, on the other hand, live in the Antarctic at the other end of the Earth.

Their most important prey are **seals**, above all the ringed seal. The polar bear often waits for hours at a breathing hole in the ice until a seal comes up for air. With its keen nose it can smell prey many kilometres away and even under a layer of snow. It eats mainly the fatty meat and blubber, which give it a lot of energy. If it finds no seals, it also eats birds' eggs, carrion or plants, but these hardly fill it up.

Polar bears are excellent **swimmers** and paddle with their large front paws. Researchers have observed polar bears swimming several hundred kilometres without a break. In autumn a pregnant female polar bear digs herself a **snow den**. There, in the middle of winter, she usually gives birth to two tiny cubs that weigh only about as much as half a litre of milk. They do not leave the den until spring, and the cubs stay with their mother for about two and a half years.

Worldwide there are an estimated 26,000 polar bears (as of 2023). The International Union for Conservation of Nature IUCN classes them as **vulnerable**. The greatest danger is **climate change**, because the sea ice melts earlier in summer and forms later in autumn. Without ice the polar bear can hardly hunt seals and has to go hungry for a long time. Since 1973 an agreement between the countries around the Arctic has protected polar bears from excessive hunting.

begriffe.erklaerung: The cold region around the North Pole with the Arctic Ocean.
Frozen sea water that floats on the Arctic Ocean.
An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
A thick layer of fat under the skin that works like a warm blanket.
An animal species whose numbers could fall sharply in the future.

gewusst: Polar bears are more likely to overheat than to get cold when they run fast.
On thermal cameras polar bears are almost invisible, because so little heat escapes to the outside.
The polar bear Knut from Berlin Zoo became world famous around 2007.

teile.einleitung: Claude Lévi-Strauss was a French ethnologist, that is, a researcher who studies peoples and cultures. He founded structuralism, a way of thinking that looks for hidden patterns behind languages, myths and family rules. He lived to be almost 101.
wichtigste: Claude Lévi-Strauss was born in Brussels in 1908 and died in Paris in 2009.
In the 1930s he taught at the University of São Paulo and did research among peoples in the interior of Brazil.
In exile in New York he met the linguist Roman Jakobson, who influenced him greatly.
He is regarded as the founder of structuralism in ethnology.
In 1949 his work “The Elementary Structures of Kinship” was published.
His travel book “Tristes Tropiques” from 1955 made him world famous.
In 1973 he was elected to the Académie française.

abschnitte.text: Claude Lévi-Strauss was born in **1908** in **Brussels** in Belgium, but grew up in Paris. He first studied philosophy and law. Later he turned to **ethnology**, the science of peoples and their cultures. He died in 2009, shortly before his 101st birthday.

In the 1930s Lévi-Strauss taught at the **University of São Paulo**. From there he travelled into the interior of Brazil and visited peoples such as the Bororo and the Nambikwara. He observed how they lived together, their customs and their art. This **fieldwork** shaped all his later thinking.

During the Second World War, as a Frenchman of Jewish origin, Lévi-Strauss had to flee and went to **New York**. There he met the linguist **Roman Jakobson**. Jakobson showed him how languages are built from sounds that only get their meaning through their differences. Lévi-Strauss applied this idea to whole cultures.

**Structuralism** assumes that there are fixed patterns behind many customs, similar to the grammar rules behind a language. In his work of 1949, Lévi-Strauss described **kinship** as a system in which families and groups exchange relationships. Later he studied hundreds of **myths** from North and South America and found recurring opposites in them, such as raw and cooked. His ideas also influenced philosophy, literary studies and psychology.

The book **“Tristes Tropiques”** from 1955 tells of his travels and is both an adventure story and a reflection on cultures. In **“The Savage Mind”** from 1962 he showed that people without writing do not think any less cleverly than others. For this he coined the term **bricolage**, putting together something new from parts that are already there. From 1959 to 1982 he taught at the Collège de France in Paris.

In 1973 Lévi-Strauss was elected to the **Académie française**, one of the highest honours in France. He argued that all cultures should be seen as being of equal value. Many experts count him among the most important thinkers of the 20th century. The Musée du quai Branly in Paris, a museum of cultures outside Europe, named a hall after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies peoples, their cultures and how they live together.
A school of thought that looks for hidden patterns and rules behind language and culture.
Research on the spot, in which you live with the people and observe them.
An old story people use to explain the world and where they come from.
French for tinkering: putting together something new from whatever happens to be available.

gewusst: The scientist was not related to the jeans brand Levi Strauss, but he was often asked about it.
“Tristes Tropiques” begins with the sentence that the author hates travelling and explorers, even though the whole book is about travel.

teile.einleitung: Chien-Shiung Wu was a Chinese-American physicist and one of the most important experimental physicists of the 20th century. With her famous experiment she proved that nature distinguishes between left and right in certain nuclear decays. Because of her importance, she was called the “First Lady of Physics”.
wichtigste: Chien-Shiung Wu was born in China in 1912 and did research in physics.
She emigrated to the USA and worked for a long time at Columbia University in New York.
During the Second World War she worked on the secret Manhattan Project.
The Wu experiment of 1956/57 proved that nature distinguishes between left and right in certain nuclear decays.
She carried out the experiment with the radioactive substance cobalt-60.
Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang received the 1957 Nobel Prize for the theory she confirmed.
In 1978 she became the first person in physics to receive the Wolf Prize.

abschnitte.text: Chien-Shiung Wu was born in 1912 in a small town near **Shanghai**. Her father campaigned for girls to be able to go to school and founded a girls' school himself. Wu studied **physics** in China and was an outstanding student. In 1936 she travelled to the USA to continue her studies.

Wu wrote her doctoral thesis at the University of California in Berkeley. Later she worked for many decades at **Columbia University** in New York. She became an expert on **beta decay**, a form of radioactivity. Her measurements were known for being especially careful and precise.

During the Second World War, Wu worked on the secret **Manhattan Project** of the USA. Its aim was to develop the first atomic bombs. Among other things, Wu helped with methods for enriching uranium and with questions about radiation detectors. After the war she went back to research in fundamental physics.

For a long time physicists believed that the laws of nature would look exactly the same in a mirror; this is called **parity**. The theorists **Tsung-Dao Lee** and **Chen Ning Yang** suspected that this was not true for beta decay. In 1956/57 Wu tested this with atoms of **cobalt-60**, which she cooled almost to absolute zero. The electrons flew off mostly in one direction, so nature did distinguish between left and right.

Lee and Yang received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in 1957, but Wu did not, even though she had confirmed the theory by experiment. Many people still see this as an injustice today. In 1978 Wu became the first person in physics to receive the **Wolf Prize**. In 1975 she became the first woman president of the American Physical Society.

Wu died in New York in 1997. She campaigned for more women to be able to study the natural sciences. Because of her importance, she was given the nickname “**First Lady of Physics**”. An asteroid and several awards bear her name today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of physics that tests the laws of nature through experiments and measurements.
The decay of atomic nuclei, which produces radiation.
The question of whether the laws of nature apply in the same way in a mirror image.
A type of radioactive decay in which an atomic nucleus gives off an electron.

gewusst: For her famous experiment, Wu had to cool the cobalt atoms to less than one degree above absolute zero.
In 2021 the USA issued a postage stamp with her picture on it.
Wu was the first woman to teach in the physics department of Princeton University.

teile.einleitung: A computer is an electronic machine that stores, processes and outputs data. It calculates at lightning speed and can display texts, pictures, music and games. Deep inside, every computer works only with the two digits 0 and 1.
wichtigste: A computer processes data according to the instructions of programs.
The processor is seen as the “brain” of the computer.
Deep inside, a computer works with the digits 0 and 1.
You type letters with the keyboard and move the pointer with the mouse.
A laptop is a portable computer that you can fold open.
Texts, pictures and numbers that a computer stores are called data.
The first working programmable computer, the Z3, was built by Konrad Zuse in 1941.

abschnitte.text: The word computer comes from the English “to compute”, that is, to **calculate**. A computer takes in data, processes it and outputs a result; this principle is called **IPO**: input, processing, output. Which task it carries out is decided by the programs, which are called **software**. The devices themselves, which you can touch, are called **hardware**.

With the **keyboard** you type letters and numbers, and with the mouse you move the pointer on the screen. On tablets and smartphones a **touchscreen** does both jobs. The screen shows results, speakers and headphones play sounds, and a printer puts texts on paper. With headphones you can listen to music without disturbing others.

The **processor**, or CPU for short, is seen as the brain of the computer; it carries out billions of calculation steps per second. The **working memory** briefly remembers what is being worked on and forgets everything when it is switched off. Data is stored permanently on the hard disk or SSD. Everything is connected on a large circuit board, the motherboard.

Deep inside, a computer knows only two states: power on or power off, that is, **1 or 0**. Such a digit is called a **bit**, and eight bits make a byte. Every letter, every colour and every sound is stored as a long row of zeros and ones. This number system is called the **binary system**.

In 1941 the German engineer **Konrad Zuse** built the Z3 in Berlin, the first working programmable computer. His next machine, the Z4, was used at ETH Zurich from 1950, at that time one of the few computers in Europe. Early computers filled whole rooms; today far more computing power fits into a smartphone. From the 1980s, personal computers arrived in offices and homes.

There are many kinds of computers: desktop computers, **laptops**, tablets, smartphones and huge supercomputers. Small computers are also found in cars, washing machines and SBB ticket machines. The Swiss National Supercomputing Centre CSCS in Lugano houses some of the fastest computers in Europe, which are used for weather forecasts, for example. If you work at a computer, you should use safe passwords and take regular breaks.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the parts of a computer that you can touch.
The programs that tell a computer what to do.
The component that carries out all the calculation steps, the brain of the computer.
The smallest unit of information; it is either 0 or 1.
Texts, pictures, numbers and sounds that a computer stores and processes.

gewusst: The English word “computer” used to mean people whose job was to do calculations.
A modern smartphone is many millions of times faster than the computers that guided the Moon landing in 1969.
The term “bug” for a computer fault became famous when a real moth was found in a computer in 1947.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Federal Institute of Metrology, or METAS for short, is Switzerland's national institute for precise measures and measurements. It makes sure that a metre, a kilogram or a second is the same everywhere in Switzerland. It also provides the country's official time with atomic clocks.
wichtigste: METAS stands for the Swiss Federal Institute of Metrology.
It is located in Wabern near Bern.
Metrology means the science of measuring.
With its atomic clocks, METAS provides the official time of Switzerland.
Scales in shops must be calibrated regularly so that nobody is cheated.
With a Kibble balance, METAS can determine the kilogram using a constant of nature.
Since 2013 METAS has been a public institution.

abschnitte.text: The word **metrology** comes from Greek and means the science of measuring. It is not to be confused with meteorology, the study of the weather. Measuring means comparing a quantity with a fixed unit, for example a length with the metre. For this to work, everyone has to use the same units. Worldwide, the **International System of Units**, abbreviated SI, applies for this.

METAS is located in **Wabern** in the municipality of Köniz near Bern. Since 2013 it has been an independent public institution of the federal government. Physicists, engineers and technicians work here in laboratories where temperature and vibrations are carefully controlled. They keep the national standards, which are the most precise reference measures in Switzerland. Companies, hospitals and laboratories can have their measuring devices checked there.

METAS runs several **atomic clocks**, which measure time extremely precisely. They use the regular vibrations of atoms, for example of caesium. Their signals produce the official time of Switzerland. This time is compared with institutes all over the world and feeds into international world time. Computers, station clocks and mobile phone networks need such precise time.

When you buy cheese in a shop, you pay by weight. That is why scales in shops must be **calibrated** regularly, so that customers are not cheated. Petrol pumps at filling stations, water meters, electricity meters and police radar devices are also checked. Many of these checks are carried out by cantonal inspectors, and METAS sets the rules for them. So you can rely on a kilo of apples in Geneva being the same as in St Gallen.

In the past the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris, the **prototype kilogram**. Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined using a constant of nature, the Planck constant. To determine it this way, you need an especially precise balance, the **Kibble balance**. It compares the weight of an object with an electromagnetic force. METAS has developed its own Kibble balance and is therefore one of only a few institutes worldwide that can do this.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of precise measuring.
To have a measuring device officially checked to see whether it measures correctly.
A very precise clock that uses the vibrations of atoms to keep time.
An especially precise reference measure for a unit.

gewusst: A good atomic clock is out by less than one second in many millions of years.
In 1875 Switzerland was one of the countries that signed the international Metre Convention.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Peter was a Swiss businessman from the canton of Vaud who was the first to make milk chocolate successfully. Thanks to his invention, Switzerland became a world-famous chocolate country. His company is now part of the Nestlé group.
wichtigste: Daniel Peter lived from 1836 to 1919 and worked in Vevey on Lake Geneva.
Before he made chocolate, he was a candle maker.
He married the daughter of the chocolate maker François-Louis Cailler.
For a long time it was difficult to combine milk with chocolate, because the water in the milk spoiled the mixture.
Using condensed milk, he made the first successful milk chocolate.
His neighbour Henri Nestlé helped him with his knowledge of milk products.
He sold his milk chocolate under the name “Gala Peter”.
In 1929 the company of Peter, Cailler and Kohler became part of Nestlé.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Peter was born in **1836** in **Moudon** in the canton of Vaud and died in Vevey in 1919. As a young man he worked as a **candle maker**. But paraffin lamps gradually replaced candles, and business became harder. He married Fanny Cailler, the daughter of the chocolate pioneer **François-Louis Cailler**, and turned to chocolate.

In the past there was only dark chocolate, which people often enjoyed as a drink. Many tried to mix in milk so that the chocolate would taste milder. But fresh milk contains a lot of **water**, and that made the chocolate mixture go mouldy or lumpy. Daniel Peter worked on this problem for many years.

The breakthrough came with **condensed milk**, that is, thickened milk with little water. His neighbour in **Vevey**, the businessman **Henri Nestlé**, knew a great deal about milk products and supported him. In 1875 Peter succeeded in making a first milk chocolate, which he then went on improving. In 1887 he launched the brand **“Gala Peter”**; the Greek word gala means milk.

Peter founded his chocolate company in Vevey in 1867. Later he joined forces with the company of Jean-Jacques Kohler, and in 1911 also with Cailler, which created Peter, Cailler, Kohler. In **1929** this company became part of **Nestlé**. The Cailler brand is still made today in Broc in the canton of Fribourg.

Milk chocolate became a huge export success and made **Swiss chocolate** famous worldwide. In 1879 Rodolphe Lindt in Bern invented **conching**, which makes chocolate melt especially smoothly. Together with pioneers such as Cailler, Suchard and Tobler, this created a strong chocolate industry. Today people in Switzerland eat a particularly large amount of chocolate per person.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thickened milk from which a large part of the water has been removed.
Chocolate made from cocoa, sugar and milk, which is lighter and milder than dark chocolate.
Stirring and warming the chocolate mixture for a long time so that it becomes fine and smooth.
Someone who founds and runs their own company.

gewusst: It took Daniel Peter about eight years before his milk chocolate really worked.
The name “Gala” comes from Greek and simply means milk.

teile.einleitung: At an inventors' competition, children, young people or adults show their own inventions. A jury judges how new, useful and well made an idea is. Anyone who takes part learns to tinker, to try things out and not to give up.
wichtigste: An invention is something new that did not exist before.
At an inventors' competition, a new idea matters most.
A first trial model of an invention is called a prototype.
A jury decides who wins the competition.
With a patent you can protect an invention in Switzerland for at most 20 years.
A big international inventions fair takes place in Geneva every year.
If a prototype does not work, you improve it and try again.

abschnitte.text: An **inventors' competition** is a competition in which inventions are presented and judged. An **invention** is something new that solves a problem or makes something easier. It can be a device, a tool, a game or an idea for protecting the environment. What matters is that the idea does not yet exist in that form. Many competitions have their own categories for children and young people.

It starts with a problem from everyday life, for example a school bag that always falls over. In an **inventor's notebook** you record ideas, sketches and experiments. Then you build a first model, the **prototype**, often out of cardboard, wood, Lego or with a 3D printer. If the prototype does not work straight away, you look for the fault, improve it and test again. Many famous inventions needed hundreds of attempts.

At the competition you present your invention at a stand or in a presentation. A **jury** of experts examines the projects. They look at whether the idea is new, whether it works and whether it is useful. A good explanation and clear documentation also count. There are often prizes, awards or contacts with companies that may develop the invention further.

In **Geneva** the International Exhibition of Inventions takes place every year, where inventors from many countries exhibit. For young people the foundation **Swiss Youth in Science** organises a national competition in which their own research and invention projects are awarded prizes. The best participants get to travel to international competitions. Many schools and municipalities also hold smaller inventors' days. Switzerland is regarded as a very inventive country, the home of the hook-and-loop fastener and the vegetable peeler, for example.

If you want to protect an invention from copycats, you can apply for a **patent**. In Switzerland the Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property in Bern is responsible for this. A patent protects an invention for at most 20 years; after that anyone may copy it. For this you have to describe the invention exactly, and it must really be new. Albert Einstein, by the way, worked as an examiner at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something new that did not exist before and that solves a problem.
A first trial model with which you test whether an idea works.
A protection right that forbids others to copy an invention without permission.
A group of experts who judge entries in a competition.

gewusst: The Swiss inventor George de Mestral invented the hook-and-loop fastener after burrs got stuck on his dog.
The Rex vegetable peeler was invented in Switzerland in 1947 and is still made almost unchanged today.
Thomas Edison is said to have remarked that he had not failed but had simply found many ways that do not work.

teile.einleitung: Electroencephalography, or EEG for short, is an examination in which the electrical activity of the brain is measured. Small electrodes are stuck onto the scalp and record tiny voltages. The traces show whether you are awake, asleep or whether the brain is working abnormally.
wichtigste: An EEG measures the electrical activity of the brain.
Hans Berger recorded the first EEG in a human being in 1924.
The electrodes are placed on the scalp.
When relaxed with the eyes closed, alpha waves typically appear.
In deep sleep, slow delta waves are typical.
The EEG is especially helpful in diagnosing epilepsy.
How fast brain waves oscillate is given in hertz.

abschnitte.text: Our brain consists of billions of **nerve cells** that communicate with electrical signals. When many nerve cells are active at the same time, tiny voltages arise that can be measured on the scalp. They are only a few millionths of a volt, so strong amplifiers are needed. The device records these voltages as wavy lines. This recording is called an **electroencephalogram**.

For a normal EEG, a cap is put on or **electrodes** are stuck onto the scalp. Usually there are about 20 electrodes, arranged according to a fixed scheme. To make sure the contact is good, a conducting gel is used. The examination does not hurt, because the device only measures and gives off no current. Sometimes you are asked to breathe deeply or to look into a flickering light.

How fast the waves oscillate is given in **hertz**, that is, oscillations per second. Someone lying awake and relaxed with their eyes closed typically shows **alpha waves** at about 8 to 13 hertz. During concentrated thinking, faster beta waves appear. In deep sleep, slow **delta waves** below 4 hertz are typical. In between there are theta waves, for example when falling asleep.

The EEG is especially important in diagnosing **epilepsy**. During an epileptic seizure, many nerve cells fire at the same time, which produces typical spikes in the EEG. In a **sleep laboratory**, the EEG is used to determine the sleep stages, for example in cases of sleep problems. Doctors also use it in intensive care and during operations. In research, people even use EEG signals to control computers without using their hands.

The German psychiatrist **Hans Berger** recorded the first EEG in a human being in Jena in 1924. However, he only published his results in 1929, because he himself was unsure for a long time. The alpha waves were at first called the Berger rhythm after him. At the beginning, many experts did not believe that brain currents could be measured. Today the EEG is standard equipment in every larger hospital.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small sensor that picks up electrical signals.
The unit for oscillations per second.
A condition in which seizures occur because of excessive nerve activity in the brain.
A cell that receives electrical signals and passes them on.

gewusst: The brain is very active during sleep too, and the EEG shows quite different wave patterns then.
When you open your eyes, the alpha waves usually disappear at once, because the brain is busy seeing.

teile.einleitung: Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who lived in Egypt more than 2,200 years ago. Using only shadows, geometry and clever thinking, he worked out the circumference of the Earth astonishingly accurately. He also invented a simple method for finding prime numbers.
wichtigste: Eratosthenes lived from about 276 to 194 BC.
He was in charge of the famous Library of Alexandria.
He calculated the circumference of the Earth using the shadow of the midday sun in Alexandria and Syene.
Syene is now called Aswan and lies in the south of Egypt.
With the sieve of Eratosthenes you can find prime numbers.
He is regarded as the founder of geography and is said to have coined its name.
Critics called him “Beta”, because in many subjects he was considered the second best.

abschnitte.text: **Eratosthenes** was born around 276 BC in Cyrene, a Greek city in what is now Libya. He studied in Athens and was then brought to Alexandria by the Egyptian king. There he was in charge of the **Library of Alexandria**, the largest collection of books in the ancient world. He worked on mathematics, astronomy, geography, history and poetry. He died around 194 BC.

Eratosthenes heard that in **Syene**, today's **Aswan**, the sun stood exactly overhead at midday on the longest day of the year. Then objects cast no shadow, and sunlight reached the bottom of a well. In Alexandria, further north, a vertical stick cast a short **shadow** at the same time. From this he calculated that the angle between the cities was about one fiftieth of a whole circle. Because the distance between the cities was about 5,000 stadia, this gave a circumference of the Earth of 250,000 stadia.

A **stadion** was an old Greek unit of length whose exact length we do not know for certain today. Depending on the conversion, Eratosthenes arrived at about 39,000 to 46,000 kilometres. The true circumference at the equator is about 40,075 kilometres. For a measurement without modern instruments, that is a splendid result. His method also shows that the scholars of the ancient world had long known that the Earth is a **sphere**.

A **prime number** is a number that can only be divided by 1 and by itself. In the **sieve of Eratosthenes** you write down all the numbers and first cross out all the multiples of 2, then those of 3, then those of 5 and so on. What is left are the prime numbers. Between 1 and 20 there remain 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19, so eight prime numbers. School pupils still learn this method today.

Eratosthenes wrote a work describing the Earth and is said to have coined the word **geography** in it. He drew a world map with lines resembling lines of longitude and latitude. He also estimated the tilt of the Earth's axis and drew up a list of stars. Because he was very good in so many subjects but never the best in all of them, critics mockingly called him **“Beta”**, after the second letter of the Greek alphabet. Others called him “Pentathlos”, like an athlete in the pentathlon who is good at many things.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of a line all the way around the Earth.
A number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and by itself.
A Greek unit of length from ancient times, roughly as long as a running track in a stadium.
The science of the Earth, its countries, landscapes and peoples.

gewusst: There is a crater on the Moon named after Eratosthenes.
The word stadium for a sports ground comes from the old unit of length, because the running track in Olympia was one stadion long.
Eratosthenes' experiment can be repeated today by school classes measuring shadows at the same time in different places.

teile.einleitung: Ethnology is the science that studies and compares cultures and societies all over the world. It asks how people live together, celebrate, work, believe and communicate. In German-speaking countries it used to be called Völkerkunde.
wichtigste: Ethnology studies and compares cultures and societies.
In German-speaking countries it used to be called Völkerkunde.
Ethnography describes a culture, while ethnology compares and explains.
The emic perspective is the view of the people of a culture themselves.
The most important method is fieldwork, in which researchers live with the people for a long time.
In 1871 Edward Burnett Tylor defined culture as “that complex whole”.
The Museum der Kulturen in Basel has one of the most important ethnographic collections in Europe.

abschnitte.text: The word **ethnology** comes from the Greek ethnos, people, and logos, study. Ethnologists study how people live in different societies. This includes family and kinship, language, religion, economy, art and festivals. Today they study not only distant villages but also big cities, clubs or internet communities. In English-speaking countries people usually speak of **cultural anthropology** or social anthropology.

**Ethnography** describes a single culture as precisely as possible. Ethnology compares many such descriptions and looks for explanations. The difference between two points of view is important. The **emic perspective** is the view of the people of the culture themselves, while the etic perspective is the view from outside. Good research tries to see the world through other people's eyes, without taking one's own culture as the measure.

The most important method is **fieldwork**. Researchers often live for months with the people they are studying, learn their language and join in everyday life. This is called **participant observation**. The method became well known through Bronisław Malinowski, who did research on the Trobriand Islands in the Pacific during the First World War. The American Clifford Geertz later made **thick description** well known, which explains not only actions but also their meaning.

In 1871 the Briton **Edward Burnett Tylor** described culture as “that complex whole” that includes knowledge, belief, art, morals and custom. **Franz Boas**, who emigrated from Germany to the USA, is regarded as the founder of American cultural anthropology. He showed that no culture is “higher” or “lower” than another. In 1925 the Frenchman Marcel Mauss wrote the “Essai sur le don” about gifts and return gifts. He showed that giving creates relationships between people everywhere in the world.

In Switzerland you can study ethnology at the universities of Basel, Bern, Zurich, Fribourg and Neuchâtel, for example. The **Museum der Kulturen Basel** holds more than 340,000 objects from all over the world. The Musée d'ethnographie in Geneva and the ethnographic museum of the University of Zurich also show fascinating collections. Today museums also ask critical questions about how objects were acquired in colonial times. Some pieces are therefore being returned to their countries of origin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything people learn together and pass on: language, customs, beliefs, art and knowledge.
Research on the spot, in which you live with the people being studied.
From the point of view of the people who belong to a culture.
The attitude of taking one's own culture as the measure for all others.

gewusst: Swiss customs such as the carnival or the bringing down of cattle from the alpine pastures are also studied by ethnologists.
Franz Boas studied the languages and cultures of the Inuit and of the peoples of the northwest coast of America.
Many ethnologists keep a diary during their fieldwork, which later becomes an important source in itself.

teile.einleitung: In ice core drilling, long cylinders of ice are pulled out of glaciers and ice sheets. The ice is like an archive in which the climate of many thousands of years is stored. Researchers from Bern are among the most important experts in the world in this field.
wichtigste: An ice core is a long column of ice taken out of the ice with a hollow drill.
In Greenland the years can often be counted from visible layers of summer and winter snow.
Tiny air bubbles in the ice contain old air with earlier CO2 and methane levels.
The ratio of oxygen isotopes reveals the temperature of the past.
In 1966 the Greenland ice was drilled through to the bedrock for the first time at Camp Century.
The Bern physicist Hans Oeschger gave his name to the Dansgaard-Oeschger events.
Ice cores from the Antarctic reach back much further than those from Greenland.

abschnitte.text: In Greenland and in the Antarctic there are huge ice sheets kilometres thick. They formed because year after year snow fell and no longer melted. Under the weight above it, the snow was pressed into **firn** and finally into ice. In **ice core drilling**, a hollow drill cuts out a round column of ice, the **ice core**. Piece by piece it is brought to the surface, often in sections a few metres long.

The layers in the ice are like the growth rings of a tree, which is why in Greenland the **annual layers** can often be counted directly. As the snow was compressed, tiny **air bubbles** were trapped. They contain real air from the past, and you can measure in them how much CO2 and methane there was at the time. The Dane Willi Dansgaard used the ratio of **oxygen isotopes** as a thermometer of the past. Dust and volcanic ash in the ice also tell of storms and volcanic eruptions.

From the 1960s the physicist **Hans Oeschger** built up a laboratory at the University of Bern that is still one of the world's leading ones today. He developed methods for measuring the air from the bubbles very precisely. Together with Dansgaard, sudden climate jumps during the ice age were discovered in Greenland ice cores. Today these are called **Dansgaard-Oeschger events**. Researchers from Bern have taken part in almost all the major drilling projects.

The first drilling down to the bedrock in Greenland succeeded in 1966 at the American military base **Camp Century**. In the early 1990s the European project **GRIP** drilled to the bottom at the summit of the Greenland ice sheet, about 3,000 metres deep. The NEEM project was meant above all to capture the **Eemian warm period** about 120,000 years ago. Since the 2010s, EastGRIP has been studying a large ice stream in northeast Greenland. In the Antarctic, the EPICA project at Dome C produced ice that is about 800,000 years old.

In the Antarctic much less snow falls each year than in Greenland, so far older layers lie on top of each other there. Ice cores show that CO2 and temperature were closely linked in the past. They also show that there is clearly more CO2 in the air today than at any time in the last 800,000 years. This makes ice cores an important piece of evidence in **climate research**. The Beyond EPICA project is even looking in the Antarctic for ice that is more than a million years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge mass of ice, several kilometres thick, that covers a whole country.
Old, grainy snow that slowly turns into glacier ice.
A kind of atom of an element that is slightly heavier or lighter than others.
Something from nature in which information about the climate of earlier times is stored.

gewusst: Ice cores are stored in freezer rooms at about minus 20 degrees or colder so that they do not melt.
If you put a piece of very old ice in water, it crackles, because the old air escapes from the bubbles.
In ice cores you find traces of volcanic eruptions that can be dated precisely.

teile.einleitung: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants; it is also called leaf green. The plant needs it to make energy from sunlight. Without chlorophyll there would be no photosynthesis and therefore no oxygen to breathe.
wichtigste: Chlorophyll is the green pigment of plants and is also called leaf green.
It is found in tiny parts of plant cells, the chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll captures sunlight, especially red and blue light.
With this energy the plant makes sugar in photosynthesis.
As a by-product, this produces the oxygen we breathe.
Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light.
In autumn the chlorophyll is broken down and yellow and red colours become visible.

abschnitte.text: The name **chlorophyll** comes from Greek and means “leaf green”. It is a pigment found in almost all plants, in algae and in some bacteria. In leaf cells it sits in small green grains, the **chloroplasts**. A single leaf cell can contain dozens of them. In the middle of a chlorophyll molecule there is an atom of the metal **magnesium**.

Sunlight is made up of many colours, as you can see in a rainbow. Chlorophyll mainly absorbs **red** and **blue** light. Green light, on the other hand, is reflected. That is why leaves, grass and forests look green to our eyes. The chlorophyll passes the light energy it has absorbed on to the plant.

With the light energy, the plant makes glucose in **photosynthesis**. To do this it takes in water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air. From the sugar it builds wood, leaves, fruit and seeds. As a by-product, **oxygen** is produced, which gets into the air through tiny openings. In this way plants provide the basis for almost all life on Earth.

abschnitte.titel: Why leaves change colour in autumn
abschnitte.text: In autumn, deciduous trees get ready for winter. They break down the valuable chlorophyll and store its building blocks in the trunk and roots. Now the yellow and orange **carotenoids**, which were in the leaf all along, become visible. Some trees also make red pigments. That is why forests in Switzerland glow yellow, orange and red in autumn.

The German chemist **Richard Willstätter** studied the structure of chlorophyll in detail. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1915. He also worked at ETH Zurich. Today chlorophyll is used as a green food colouring, for example in sweets. Researchers are trying to copy photosynthesis in order to make fuel from sunlight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny green grain in plant cells in which photosynthesis takes place.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.
Yellow and orange pigments in plants, for example in carrots.
A substance that colours something because it absorbs certain colours of light.

gewusst: The red pigment in our blood is built very much like chlorophyll, but it has iron in the middle instead of magnesium.
Plants that sprout in the dark are a yellowish white, because without light they hardly make any chlorophyll.

teile.einleitung: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist. He developed the theory of evolution by natural selection and used it to explain how living things change over very long periods of time. His ideas are among the most important in the whole of biology.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin lived in England from 1809 to 1882.
From 1831 to 1836 he sailed around the world on the ship HMS Beagle.
On the Galápagos Islands he observed finches with different beaks.
He developed the theory of evolution by natural selection.
In 1859 his famous book “On the Origin of Species” was published.
Alfred Russel Wallace came to similar conclusions independently of him.
Darwin was buried in Westminster Abbey in London.

abschnitte.text: **Charles Darwin** was born on 12 February 1809 in Shrewsbury in England. His father was a doctor and wanted Charles to study medicine too. But Charles preferred collecting beetles and observing nature. Later he studied theology in Cambridge. There he met naturalists who encouraged his enthusiasm.

In 1831 the young Darwin was allowed to travel on the survey ship **HMS Beagle**. The voyage lasted almost five years and went all the way around the world. Darwin collected plants, animals, rocks and fossils in South America, Australia and on many islands. The **Galápagos Islands** in the Pacific were especially important. There he saw that finches and tortoises differed from island to island.

Darwin realised that living things of the same species differ slightly from one another. Those that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and have more young. These features are passed on to the young. In this way species change over many generations. Darwin called this process **natural selection**, and it leads to **evolution**.

Darwin worked on his theory for more than 20 years before he published it. In 1858 he learned that **Alfred Russel Wallace** had come to similar ideas independently. Both presented their ideas together in 1858. In 1859 Darwin's book “On the Origin of Species” was published and sold out immediately. In 1871 it was followed by a book on **the descent of man**.

Darwin's ideas caused fierce debates, because many people believed that species never changed. Today the **theory of evolution** is the foundation of modern biology. It has been confirmed many times by fossil finds and by genetics. Darwin died on 19 April 1882 at his home in Kent. He was buried in **Westminster Abbey** in London.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
The better adapted living things survive and reproduce more often.
A group of living things that can reproduce with one another.
Remains or traces of living things from earlier times that have turned to stone.

gewusst: The finches of the Galápagos Islands are now called Darwin's finches in honour of the scientist.
Darwin suffered from seasickness almost the whole time on the voyage of the Beagle.

teile.einleitung: The Declaration of Helsinki is a set of principles for medical research on people. The World Medical Association adopted it in 1964 in the Finnish capital, Helsinki. It is meant to make sure that people who take part in studies are protected and respected.
wichtigste: The Declaration of Helsinki was adopted by the World Medical Association in 1964.
It sets out the ethics of medical research on people.
The well-being of the individual research participant comes before the interests of science and society.
Participants must be well informed and agree voluntarily.
An independent ethics committee must check the research plan before the study begins.
Studies should be registered before the first person takes part, and negative results should also be published.
Since 1964 the declaration has been revised several times.

abschnitte.text: The **Declaration of Helsinki** is a kind of rulebook for doctors and researchers. It describes how new medicines and treatments may be tested on people without putting the participants at risk. It was adopted by the **World Medical Association**, an alliance of doctors' organisations from many countries. It is not a law, but many countries have included its principles in their laws.

After the Second World War it became known that during the Nazi era experiments had been carried out on people without their consent. As a result, the **Nuremberg Code** was drawn up in 1947 with the first rules for experiments on people. The World Medical Association built on this and adopted its own declaration in **Helsinki** in **1964**. Since then it has been revised several times so that it fits new questions in medicine.

At its centre is the **well-being of the individual participant**, which comes before the interests of science and society. Every person must be told in an understandable way about the aims, benefits and risks. Only then may they agree voluntarily; this is called **informed consent**. They may drop out again at any time without any disadvantage.

Before a study begins, an independent **ethics committee** must check the research plan. Every study should be entered in a public register before the first person takes part. In addition, **all results** should be published, including negative or unclear ones. That way nobody can show only the good results and hide the bad ones.

A **placebo** is a dummy medicine without an active ingredient, used to compare new medicines against. Its use is especially controversial when a proven treatment already exists. In that case, sick people in the placebo group would miss out on an effective treatment. The declaration therefore only allows placebos under strict conditions.

In Switzerland, the **Human Research Act** regulates research on people, and it is based on similar principles. Several cantonal and regional ethics committees here check numerous studies every year.
